1c32428a-dac7-4d7f-8359-e4d4946f692d.paper_title: Association between hypothyroidism, levothyroxine replacement and kidney function outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
1c32428a-dac7-4d7f-8359-e4d4946f692d.text:
In clinical practice, patients with severe overt hypothyroidism are at high risk of kidney dysfunction. Two Mendelian randomization studies have demonstrated a significant causal association between hypothyroidism and CKD ( 9 , 10 ). This association has also been reported in previous high-quality observational studies ( 11 – 13 ). However, some confusion remains in this field. First, the associations between SHypo and kidney outcomes require further confirmation. Second, it is currently unclear what effect levothyroxine (LT4) has on kidney-related clinical outcomes in hypothyroidism patients. Third, differences in participants’ age, gender, race, etc., can lead to inconsistent findings in previous studies. Fourth, the reference intervals for thyroid function and parameters or formulas for kidney function were inconsistent across the studies. Studies on the above topic have been continuously reported over the past two decades. However, a systematic review and meta-analysis summarizing their findings is lacking.

The purpose of this study was to comprehensively elucidate the associations between hypothyroidism (especially SHypo) and kidney outcomes and to explore the changes in kidney outcomes after LT4 replacement in hypothyroidism patients.

eb3effd4-4ed6-4142-b29d-7c7e188497f8.paper_title: Association between hypothyroidism, levothyroxine replacement and kidney function outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
eb3effd4-4ed6-4142-b29d-7c7e188497f8.text: The PubMed, Cochrane Library, EMBASE, and Google Scholar databases were searched for observational studies and randomized clinical trials (RCTs). A total of three researchers were responsible for the literature search. The retrieval formula was as follows: ((renal function [All Fields]) OR (kidney function [All Fields])) AND (((((hypothyroidism [All Fields]) OR (hypothyroid [All Fields])) OR (LT4 [All Fields])) OR (L-thyroxine [All Fields])) OR (levothyroxine)). The three researchers sent the records to a fourth researcher, who then screened out duplicate records. Additionally, another researcher was tasked with scanning references in review articles to collect records that were not yet discovered by the above researchers. Through the above process, we initially included a total of 601 studies.

4f3690de-9771-4c0b-935a-869a5aace601.paper_title: Association between hypothyroidism, levothyroxine replacement and kidney function outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
4f3690de-9771-4c0b-935a-869a5aace601.heading_path: Methods > Inclusion and exclusion criteria for the studies
4f3690de-9771-4c0b-935a-869a5aace601.text: The inclusion criteria for the studies are described below. First, the clinical outcomes included the crude prevalence or incidence of CKD, or one or more biochemical tests reflecting kidney function. Second, the number of cases or incidence events of CKD and the means and SDs of continuous variables were available. Third, the confirmation of hypothyroidism was newly-diagnosed and based on laboratory measurements rather than personal history collection. Fourth, the etiology of hypothyroidism must be primary, not central or iatrogenic, to minimize the influence of other types of thyroid diseases or irrelevant treatments on kidney function. Fifth, the researchers explicitly reported that the serum TSH levels returned to the euthyroid range after LT4 replacement.

3167acb4-095b-4e38-aaa8-e19dc45bc30c.paper_title: Association between hypothyroidism, levothyroxine replacement and kidney function outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
3167acb4-095b-4e38-aaa8-e19dc45bc30c.text: The Newcastle–Ottawa Scale was selected for quality evaluation ( 15 ). The scale for case–control studies was applied when kidney outcomes in participants with different thyroid function statuses were compared. The scale used in cohort studies was referred to when analyzing the effects of LT4 replacement on kidney outcomes in patients with hypothyroidism. Briefly, the scale for case–control studies include the following three items: selection of individuals, comparability between the hypothyroidism patients and the non-hypothyroidism controls, and confirmation of the diagnosis of hypothyroidism. The scale for cohort studies includes the following three items: selection of hypothyroidism patients, intergroup comparability between hypothyroidism patients and control individuals, and selection and assessment of kidney outcomes. The maximum score for both scales is nine. Only studies with a score of five or above were considered for inclusion in this meta-analysis. After the screening process shown in Figure 1 , all the candidate studies met the criteria and could be used for further analysis.

55b5d92b-2657-4df2-9f3d-5dc1ba548a07.paper_title: Association between hypothyroidism, levothyroxine replacement and kidney function outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
55b5d92b-2657-4df2-9f3d-5dc1ba548a07.text: A preliminary literature search revealed a paucity of epidemiological studies examining the impact of overt hypothyroidism on kidney outcomes. In addition, given the well-established association between overt hypothyroidism and kidney dysfunction in practice, we did not consider patients with overt hypothyroidism as a distinct subgroup in the present study. The independent variables in this study were overall hypothyroidism without distinction, as well as SHypo.

6d30ea84-321a-4f33-b6b3-e2e3486aa803.paper_title: Association between hypothyroidism, levothyroxine replacement and kidney function outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
6d30ea84-321a-4f33-b6b3-e2e3486aa803.text: Two independent investigators extracted the means, SDs, and numbers of participants for each kidney outcome. For kidney outcomes presented as continuous variables, the inverse variance method was used to analyze the association between hypothyroidism or LT4 replacement and the outcome, and the standard mean difference (SMD) was regarded as the effect variable. For kidney outcomes presented as dichotomous variables, the Mantel–Haenszel method was used, and odds ratios (ORs) or risk ratios (RRs) were applied as the effect variables. The heterogeneity among the studies was estimated with the chi-square-based Q test and the I 2 test; I 2 ≤ 50% and I 2 > 50% corresponded to a fixed-effects model and a random-effects model, respectively. Unless otherwise specified, sensitivity analysis was conducted by the sequential removal of the studies. The meta-analysis was performed by using Review Manager (Version 5.4.1; The Cochrane Collaboration, 2020). Publication bias was assessed by using Egger test plots in Stata 16 (Stata Corp, College Station, TX).

26700a9c-72ec-4bbe-8500-132a9a699112.paper_title: Association between hypothyroidism, levothyroxine replacement and kidney function outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
26700a9c-72ec-4bbe-8500-132a9a699112.heading_path: Results > Characteristics of the included studies
26700a9c-72ec-4bbe-8500-132a9a699112.text:
In total, 46 studies, covering more than 800,000 individuals, were included in the meta-analysis of the associations between hypothyroidism and kidney outcomes ( 11 – 13 , 16 – 58 ). As shown in Table 1 , the time span of the studies ranged from 1998 to 2025. Among these studies, 18 did not differentiate the severity of hypothyroidism, 18 merely analyzed the associations between SHypo and kidney outcomes, and nine studies differentiated the severity of hypothyroidism.

Additionally, nine studies examined changes in kidney function before and after LT4 replacement ( Table 2 ) ( 20 , 30 , 39 , 59 – 64 ). Changes in serum creatinine levels and the eGFR were also assessed. These studies were small-sample prospective studies with follow-up durations ranging from three months to three years.

f681c695-d8f2-4c5d-98d8-1058a02b155b.paper_title: Association between hypothyroidism, levothyroxine replacement and kidney function outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
f681c695-d8f2-4c5d-98d8-1058a02b155b.heading_path: Results > Associations between hypothyroidism and the prevalence of CKD and ESRD
f681c695-d8f2-4c5d-98d8-1058a02b155b.text:
As shown in Figure 2 , pooled hypothyroidism was associated with a higher risk of CKD (OR 1.94, 95% CI [1.62, 2.32], P < 0.00001). Subgroup analysis revealed that SHypo and non-distinct hypothyroidism were positively associated with CKD (OR 1.87, 95% CI [1.55, 2.27], P < 0.0001; OR 1.98, 95% CI [1.36, 2.89], P = 0.0004, respectively).

As shown in Supplementary Figure 1 , overall, hypothyroidism was associated with a higher risk of ESRD (OR 1.92, 95% CI [1.23, 2.99], P = 0.004). Subgroup analysis was conducted based on the presence of prior kidney dysfunction, and the results suggested that hypothyroidism remained significantly associated with ESRD in the general population (OR 3.16, 95% CI [1.58, 6.35], P = 0.001). However, no evidence of an association between hypothyroidism and ESRD was found among participants who already had CKD.

4988a0fd-366a-42bb-ac7d-d005eeacd551.heading_path: Results > Association between hypothyroidism and the incidence of CKD
4988a0fd-366a-42bb-ac7d-d005eeacd551.text: Three cohort studies included 4,042 patients with varying severities of hypothyroidism. As shown in Supplementary Figure 2 , no significant association was found between hypothyroidism and the CKD incidence.

194c4182-6069-411a-8b69-1fbacf45007f.paper_title: Association between hypothyroidism, levothyroxine replacement and kidney function outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
194c4182-6069-411a-8b69-1fbacf45007f.heading_path: Results > Associations between hypothyroidism and the biochemical parameters of kidney function
194c4182-6069-411a-8b69-1fbacf45007f.text:
Nine case-control studies, which included 936 patients, compared serum urea levels between patients with hypothyroidism and controls ( Supplementary Figure 3 ). Overall, hypothyroidism was associated with elevated serum urea levels according to pooled data from the two subgroups (SMD 0.47, 95% CI [0.01, 0.93], P = 0.04), whereas SHypo was not significantly associated with serum urea levels.

Given the variability in baseline kidney function across the populations in the above analysis, studies that were specifically conducted in patients with underlying kidney dysfunction were removed from the sensitivity analysis. As shown in Supplementary Figure 4 , the above conclusions remained robust. Pooled hypothyroidism was significantly associated with elevated serum urea levels (SMD 0.74, 95% CI [0.08, 1.39], P = 0.03), whereas SHypo was not.

53baa8f2-f1de-4be2-bbff-cf597a76640c.heading_path: Results > Association between hypothyroidism and the eGFR
53baa8f2-f1de-4be2-bbff-cf597a76640c.text: As shown in Figure 3 , the cross-sectional association between hypothyroidism and the eGFR was investigated in 20 studies. Twelve and eight studies were conducted in patients with SHypo and hypothyroidism without distinction, respectively. There was a significant association between hypothyroidism and a decreased eGFR (SMD -0.68, 95% CI [-0.81, -0.55], P < 0.00001) if all the hypothyroidism cases were pooled. Subgroup analysis suggested that SHypo and hypothyroidism without distinction were also significantly associated with a decreased eGFR (SMD -0.99, 95% CI [-1.59, -0.38], P = 0.001 and SMD -0.27, 95% CI [-0.33, -0.21], P < 0.00001, respectively).

f16a1217-96da-4688-be1e-19cc63da6951.paper_title: Association between hypothyroidism, levothyroxine replacement and kidney function outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
f16a1217-96da-4688-be1e-19cc63da6951.heading_path: Results > Effects of LT4 replacement on kidney outcomes in hypothyroidism patients
f16a1217-96da-4688-be1e-19cc63da6951.text:
Serum creatinine levels were assessed in six studies. As shown in Supplementary Figure 8 , overall, serum creatinine levels in hypothyroidism patients decreased significantly after LT4 replacement (SMD -0.85, 95% CI [-1.53, -0.17], P = 0.01). However, serum creatinine levels in SHypo patients did not significantly differ from baseline.

Three and eight studies analyzed changes in the eGFR after LT4 treatment in patients with SHypo only and hypothyroidism without distinction, respectively. As shown in Supplementary Figure 9 , we did not find an explicit effect of LT4 replacement on the eGFR in pooled hypothyroidism patients.

9a3b2384-6ba7-42e0-8b1c-ea1d84306f7e.paper_title: Association between hypothyroidism, levothyroxine replacement and kidney function outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
9a3b2384-6ba7-42e0-8b1c-ea1d84306f7e.text: To our knowledge, no meta-analysis investigating the association of hypothyroidism and specific kidney outcomes have been published so far, thus this study would be of high clinical significance. This study verified that hypothyroidism (including SHypo) was significantly associated with the prevalence of CKD and reduced eGFR. Furthermore, hypothyroidism was also significantly cross-sectionally associated with increased serum urea and serum creatinine. These conclusions are consistent with our previous experience in clinical practice. However, this study concluded that hypothyroidism was not associated with the incidence of CKD or the progression of ESRD in subjects with prior CKD. LT4 treatment was not associated with improvement in eGFR, either in non-distinct hypothyroidism or in SHypo patients.

9f1c86bc-c7ef-4eee-a16d-5fe27a4276e1.paper_title: Association between hypothyroidism, levothyroxine replacement and kidney function outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
9f1c86bc-c7ef-4eee-a16d-5fe27a4276e1.text: This study conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of studies on hypothyroidism and kidney outcomes based on evidence from the past two decades. Both non-distinct hypothyroidism and SHypo were found to be cross-sectionally associated with CKD and a reduced eGFR. However, hypothyroidism did not appear to be significantly associated with the incidence or further progression of CKD. No significant increase in eGFR was observed after LT4 replacement was given to patients with non-distinct hypothyroidism or SHypo to restore euthyroidism. Further consideration and exploration of the bidirectional relationships between hypothyroidism and kidney outcomes are warranted, as this will have substantial benefits for the management of hypothyroidism and CKD.

d10dd2f4-ad28-431a-877c-e4c47819e28f.paper_title: Renal Biomarkers of Injury as Early Predictors of COVID-19 Associated Acute Kidney Injury: A Prospective Observational Trial (BRICOAKI Study)
d10dd2f4-ad28-431a-877c-e4c47819e28f.text: Acute kidney injury has emerged as a major determinant of morbidity and mortality in critically ill patients with COVID-19. Reported AKI incidence ranges from 20 to 80% in intensive care unit (ICU) settings and is associated with prolonged hospitalization, need for RRT, and increased mortality. 1 – 3 Multiple mechanisms contribute to AKI in COVID-19, including direct viral cytopathic effects via angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE)-2 receptors in renal tissue, endothelial injury, cytokine-mediated tubular damage, microthrombi, and renal hypoperfusion. 4 – 6 However, early diagnosis remains challenging because serum creatinine is a late functional marker and may not reflect the onset of injury. Urine-output criteria can be affected by factors like diuretics (as the clinician is supposed to maintain intravascular volume and perfusion pressure). 7

Reported AKI incidence ranges from 20 to 80% in intensive care unit (ICU) settings and is associated with prolonged hospitalization, need for RRT, and increased mortality. 1 – 3 Multiple mechanisms contribute to AKI in COVID-19, including direct viral cytopathic effects via angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE)-2 receptors in renal tissue, endothelial injury, cytokine-mediated tubular damage, microthrombi, and renal hypoperfusion. 4 – 6 However, early diagnosis remains challenging because serum creatinine is a late functional marker and may not reflect the onset of injury. Urine-output criteria can be affected by factors like diuretics (as the clinician is supposed to maintain intravascular volume and perfusion pressure). 7

This study narrows the gap by serially measuring seven functional, inflammatory, and structural renal biomarkers, conducting time-resolved ROC analysis, and estimating biomarker–creatinine lead time for COVID-19–associated AKI in an ICU cohort.

RR > 30/min, respiratory distress, SpO 2 < 90% on room air or PaO 2 /FiO 2 < 200 mm Hg.

All consecutive adult aged ≥18 years hospitalized patients with reverse transcriptase-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) confirmed moderate and severe COVID-19 patients requiring ICU admission were enrolled in this study cohort. A smaller comparator group of mild COVID-19 patients was also included for descriptive biomarker comparison. We excluded any patient with pre-existing AKI, CKD stage 4 or 5 (eGFR < 20 mL/min/1.73 m 2 ), end-stage renal disease (ESRD) on chronic dialysis, kidney transplantation within the past 12 months, or pregnancy.

For biomarker sampling, blood and urine samples were collected at different standardized time points as follows:

In patients with moderate–severe COVID-19, study group sampling was performed on days 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, and 10. In patients with mild COVID-19 (control group), sampling was performed on days 0, 3, and 10 or on the day of clinical deterioration.

Samples were centrifuged (2000 × gm, 15 min) and stored at −80°C until batch biomarker analysis.

a7950e79-ba23-48d9-b6e2-aed87feb1230.text:
The demographic characteristics were comparable across groups, except weight, which was significantly higher in moderate cases compared to severe cases ( p = 0.02). Age and sex distribution did not significantly differ between severity groups. The demographic and baseline clinical characteristics of the study population are summarized in Table 1 . The cohort was predominantly male, with a mean age of 56.3 ± 12.7 years. A total of 65 patients with confirmed COVID-19 pneumonia requiring ICU admission were included, comprising 24 moderate and 41 severe cases at baseline.

Acute kidney injury developed in 47 of 65 patients (72.3%) during ICU stay, and the onset occurred most commonly between days 2 and 5 of hospitalization. Among these, 11 patients (23.4%) developed KDIGO stage 1 AKI, 36 patients (76.6%) progressed to KDIGO stage 2 and 3, and five patients (10.6%) required RRT, and seven patients (10.7%) died, of whom three deaths (42.9%) were directly attributable to severe AKI and multiorgan dysfunction.

The demographic characteristics were comparable across groups, except weight, which was significantly higher in moderate cases compared to severe cases ( p = 0.02). Age and sex distribution did not significantly differ between severity groups. The demographic and baseline clinical characteristics of the study population are summarized in Table 1 . The cohort was predominantly male, with a mean age of 56.3 ± 12.7 years. A total of 65 patients with confirmed COVID-19 pneumonia requiring ICU admission were included, comprising 24 moderate and 41 severe cases at baseline.

Acute kidney injury developed in 47 of 65 patients (72.3%) during ICU stay, and the onset occurred most commonly between days 2 and 5 of hospitalization. Among these, 11 patients (23.4%) developed KDIGO stage 1 AKI, 36 patients (76.6%) progressed to KDIGO stage 2 and 3, and five patients (10.6%) required RRT, and seven patients (10.7%) died, of whom three deaths (42.9%) were directly attributable to severe AKI and multiorgan dysfunction.

Serum kidney injury molecule-1 showed a borderline trend toward elevation across severity categories ( p = 0.0567), whereas uKlotho did not demonstrate significant discriminatory variation ( p = 0.3566).

165b2249-7da4-4d3a-b5ca-da01ee31fca3.text:
The principal finding of this prospective ICU cohort study is that serial sNGAL and sCystatin-C levels show the strongest association with KDIGO-defined AKI in critically ill COVID-19 patients and tend to rise approximately 1–2 days before creatinine-based diagnosis, while sKIM 1, sTIMP 2, sIL 6, and uKlotho generally increase only at or after AKI onset. All analyses should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating because of the modest sample size and single-center design.

Serum NGAL demonstrated the earliest rise (~24–48 hours before KDIGO-defined AKI). Serum NGAL is released from injured distal tubular epithelial cells in response to inflammation and ischemic stress. 3 , 16 , 17 In COVID-19, tubular injury may be driven by viral tropism for ACE-2-expressing renal epithelium, microvascular endothelial injury, and cytokine-mediated mitochondrial dysfunction. 4 Our findings align with previous multicenter evaluations identifying sNGAL as a strong earlier risk identification and prognostic marker in both septic and COVID-19-associated AKI. 9 , 18 , 19

a8934660-fad0-44de-b5bb-7532e54758e4.paper_title: Renal Biomarkers of Injury as Early Predictors of COVID-19 Associated Acute Kidney Injury: A Prospective Observational Trial (BRICOAKI Study)
a8934660-fad0-44de-b5bb-7532e54758e4.text: Our study also had several limitations. It was a single-center study design, which may limit the generalizability; our sample size was modest, particularly for RRT and mortality subgroup analysis. Because AKI staging itself determines RRT initiation and contributes strongly to mortality, biomarker associations with these secondary outcomes are susceptible to circularity and residual confounding by overall disease severity (e.g., ventilatory support, vasopressor use), which were not fully adjusted for in this exploratory analysis. The urinary cell-cycle arrest biomarkers (TIMP-2)-(IGFBP7) were not measured due to assay and cost constraints. In our cohort, all AKI cases were diagnosed based on serum creatinine rise rather than urine-output criteria, which introduces inherent circularity when evaluating biomarkers that precede creatinine elevation. This should be considered when interpreting the lead-time analysis. Most prior studies evaluating early AKI biomarkers have focused on urinary measurements; therefore, direct comparison with serum-based markers should be interpreted cautiously.

0adcf687-8818-4aaf-8e38-b8fab3393c1e.paper_title: Renal Biomarkers of Injury as Early Predictors of COVID-19 Associated Acute Kidney Injury: A Prospective Observational Trial (BRICOAKI Study)
0adcf687-8818-4aaf-8e38-b8fab3393c1e.text: In critically ill COVID-19 patients, serial sNGAL and sCystatin-C measurements show modest but consistent discrimination for KDIGO-defined AKI and tend to rise 1–2 days before creatinine-based diagnosis. These biomarkers may help identify patients at increased risk of AKI progression, but the observed associations are confounded by illness severity, and the small sample precludes causal inference regarding clinical outcomes. These biomarkers should be considered adjunctive risk-stratification tools rather than diagnostic markers.

7d215094-fe1c-45d9-a94e-29ff33aaaa4c.text: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most common type of liver cancer, which is the third leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide, with its incidence and mortality rates continuing to rise. 1 , 2 The 5-year survival rate for HCC remains poor, and only a small number of patients are eligible for curative treatments (such as ablation, surgical resection, and liver transplantation), 2 as the majority of HCC patients are diagnosed at an unresectable stage. To date, the treatment of unresectable HCC remains a significant challenge.

9b1a6a19-690e-449e-b376-b63c51716e99.paper_title: Hepatic immune prognostic index as a prognostic biomarker in hepatocellular carcinoma patients treated with transarterial chemoembolization
9b1a6a19-690e-449e-b376-b63c51716e99.text: Hepatic immune prognostic index (HIPI) status (high or low) was determined by NLR and AFP levels. According to prior studies, 18 , 19 the cutoff value for NLR was 3. The AFP cutoff was 20 ng/mL, which was based on previous studies. 20 , 21 These cutoffs were chosen based on established clinical relevance and broad acceptance in hepatology guidelines. An NLR of 3 is a widely accepted threshold indicating a systemic shift toward a pro-tumor inflammatory state. 22 An AFP of 20 ng/mL is the most widely used diagnostic and risk-stratification cutoff in clinical practice, such as in the AASLD guidelines. 20 While statistical methods such as median values were also explored, these established clinical thresholds were chosen to ensure the index’s practical applicability in real-world clinical settings. NLR < 3 and AFP < 20 ng/mL were defined as HIPI-low, and NLR ⩾3 or AFP ⩾20 ng/mL as HIPI-high.

a7867882-cac2-4a11-970d-f99fe4d82d52.paper_title: Hepatic immune prognostic index as a prognostic biomarker in hepatocellular carcinoma patients treated with transarterial chemoembolization
a7867882-cac2-4a11-970d-f99fe4d82d52.heading_path: Materials and methods > Follow-up and assessment
a7867882-cac2-4a11-970d-f99fe4d82d52.text: The first follow-up imaging was conducted 4–6 weeks after the initial TACE treatment to evaluate early tumor response and the need for additional on-demand TACE sessions. For patients with stable disease (SD), subsequent regular follow-ups were recommended every 8–12 weeks. Each follow-up included a contrast-enhanced CT scan or contrast-enhanced liver MRI, chest CT, blood biochemistry analyses, and other examinations as clinically indicated. Tumor response was evaluated using contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI according to the modified Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors. The best objective tumor response was evaluated by two independent, experienced radiologists who were blinded to the patients’ HIPI status and clinical outcomes. The disease control rate (DCR) was defined as the percentage of patients with a complete response (CR), partial response (PR), and SD; the objective response rate (ORR) was the percentage of patients with CR and PR. The overall survival (OS) was calculated from the initial treatment date until the occurrence of death or last follow-up. The progression-free survival (PFS) was defined as the time from initial treatment to tumor progression or death.

ae85242e-c60f-4287-8608-da2ec2d23bec.heading_path: Results > Baseline characteristics of the study patients
ae85242e-c60f-4287-8608-da2ec2d23bec.text: A total of 663 HCC patients who received TACE treatment were included in this study. Among the 663 patients, 538 were classified into the HIPI-high group and 125 into the HIPI-low group ( Supplemental Figure 1 ). The baseline demographic and clinical characteristics of the patients before and after PSM are summarized in Table 1 . Prior to matching, significant imbalances were observed between the two groups in several key prognostic factors, including Child–Pugh class ( p < 0.001), BCLC grade ( p < 0.001), tumor size ( p < 0.001), macrovascular invasion ( p < 0.001), white blood cell count ( p < 0.001), alanine aminotransferase (ALT; p = 0.002), total bilirubin (TBIL; p = 0.015), and albumin (ALB; p < 0.001). To reduce these differences and achieve balance, PSM was performed, resulting in 113 well-matched pairs.

cc339b50-b2ea-48f4-bc9b-36b3fb019da1.paper_title: Hepatic immune prognostic index as a prognostic biomarker in hepatocellular carcinoma patients treated with transarterial chemoembolization
cc339b50-b2ea-48f4-bc9b-36b3fb019da1.text: Based on the tumor response evaluation following TACE treatment, significant differences were observed between the HIPI-low and HIPI-high groups both before and after PSM ( Table 2 ). Prior to matching, the ORR and DCR were significantly higher in the HIPI-low group than in the HIPI-high group (ORR: 64.0% vs 31.6%, p < 0.001; DCR: 86.4% vs 68.4%, p < 0.001). After PSM, the ORR and DCR in the HIPI-low group were significantly higher than those in the HIPI-high group (ORR: 63.7% vs 41.6%, p = 0.001; DCR: 86.7% vs 71.7%, p = 0.005).

5147b7cb-d462-46e8-a50e-a420941487c2.paper_title: Hepatic immune prognostic index as a prognostic biomarker in hepatocellular carcinoma patients treated with transarterial chemoembolization
5147b7cb-d462-46e8-a50e-a420941487c2.text: The median follow-up time was 22.0 months (IQR, 17.0–29.0 months). Kaplan–Meier survival curves demonstrated significantly worse survival outcomes in HIPI-high patients than in HIPI-low patients, both before and after PSM ( Figure 1 ). Before PSM, the median OS in the HIPI-low group was significantly longer than that in the HIPI-high group (26.0 vs 12.4 months, p < 0.001; Figure 1(a) ), and the median PFS was also significantly longer in the HIPI-low group (9.4 vs 5.5 months, p < 0.001; Figure 1(b) ). 3ce42e0e-4aa8-4ac4-86fa-8f36be86df59.paper_title: Hepatic immune prognostic index as a prognostic biomarker in hepatocellular carcinoma patients treated with transarterial chemoembolization
3ce42e0e-4aa8-4ac4-86fa-8f36be86df59.text: Subgroup analyses based on baseline characteristics in the PSM cohort revealed consistent trends for OS and PFS. In the OS analysis ( Figure 2 ), a significant interaction was identified between ascites status and HIPI group ( p for interaction = 0.023). The HIPI-high status was associated with inferior OS regardless of ascites status; however, this effect was more pronounced in patients with ascites (HR, 4.20; 95% CI, 1.34–13.20). Although the difference did not reach statistical significance in some subgroups, high HIPI status was consistently correlated with worse OS across other subgroups. For PFS ( Figure 3 ), a significant interaction was observed between tumor size and HIPI group ( p for interaction = 0.019), with a more substantial increase in PFS risk for tumors >10 cm (HR, 3.98; 95% CI, 1.27–12.46). In addition, among patients with ascites or distant metastasis, those in the HIPI-high group showed a nonsignificant trend toward lower PFS risk than those in the HIPI-low group. In all other subgroups, high HIPI status was uniformly associated with poorer PFS outcomes, even when statistical significance was not reached in certain subsets.

37d219ac-53fd-4da4-9399-e7cbe9d490e7.paper_title: Hepatic immune prognostic index as a prognostic biomarker in hepatocellular carcinoma patients treated with transarterial chemoembolization
37d219ac-53fd-4da4-9399-e7cbe9d490e7.text:

a0891de5-f6b1-43bb-985c-7a5d12ed6e84.paper_title: Weil's disease: rapid recovery following corticosteroid treatment: a case report
a0891de5-f6b1-43bb-985c-7a5d12ed6e84.text:
Leptospirosis is a zoonotic disease caused by pathogenic spirochetes of the genus Leptospira . Infection occurs via direct or indirect contact with the urine or tissues of infected animals. The estimated annual number of cases worldwide exceeds one million, with approximately 59,000 deaths reported each year 1 .

Although cattle, pigs, horses, and dogs may also serve as reservoirs, rodents play the most significant role in transmitting the disease to humans. Transmission typically occurs through contact with water or soil contaminated with the urine of infected animals. Spirochetes usually enter the human body through mucous membranes or broken skin 2 , 3 .

Incubation period averages 5–14 days, with cases of up to 30 days having been reported. The disease may initially present nonspecific symptoms, and most patients have a favorable prognosis. However, a severe clinical course is observed in approximately 10% of cases which may develop jaundice, arrhythmias, bleeding, hemodynamic instability, liver failure, pulmonary failure, renal failure, and aseptic meningitis. The case fatality rate among patients with severe disease ranges from 5% to 15% 1 , 4 .
a0891de5-f6b1-43bb-985c-7a5d12ed6e84.journal: Revista do Instituto de Medicina Tropical de São Paulo

4a900d36-8fe0-43d6-9d4e-eeb0a6108a28.text:
A 41-year-old male patient presented to the emergency department with complaints of diarrhea, vomiting, myalgia, and jaundice that had started four days earlier. His medical history revealed that he lived in the city center, worked as a carpenter, had been fishing in a stream one week earlier, and had consumed wild mushrooms two days prior to admission. He reported that his symptoms had begun approximately one week earlier and had progressively worsened, with the development of jaundice and decreased urine output over the last two days. He had no known chronic medical conditions but had a history of intravenous drug use and regular alcohol consumption.

On physical examination, his blood pressure was 110/60 mmHg, pulse rate was 130 beats/min, and body temperature was 37.8 °C. The patient's general condition was stable. The skin and sclerae were icteric. Apart from right upper quadrant tenderness, no abnormal findings were detected on physical examination. There were no signs of meningeal irritation or focal neurological deficits.
4a900d36-8fe0-43d6-9d4e-eeb0a6108a28.journal: Revista do Instituto de Medicina Tropical de São Paulo

Although leptospirosis is generally known to have a favorable course, it should not be overlooked as it can lead to severe complications and death. Failure to recognize the disease in its early stages or include it in the differential diagnosis negatively affects prognosis. In patients with suspected leptospirosis, starting antimicrobial treatment as soon as possible, without waiting for the results of diagnostic tests, is effective in reducing the severity and duration of the infection 1 .

Although the mechanism of jaundice development in leptospirosis is not fully understood, it is thought that leptospires attack hepatocytes in the liver, causing damage that leads to bile leakage from the bile ducts into the sinusoidal blood vessels, resulting in high conjugated bilirubin levels 13 . A review of the literature reveals at least one case of leptospirosis with a total bilirubin level reaching 74.3 mg/dL 14 .

73f421e2-4c31-4d87-94a0-efe514c420b5.text: Our case demonstrates that the microagglutination test may be negative in the early stages of leptospirosis and that a detailed history and strong clinical suspicion are decisive in establishing the diagnosis. Moreover, the persistence of hyperbilirubinemia and thrombocytopenia despite standard antibiotic and supportive treatment suggests that immune-mediated mechanisms may play a role in the pathogenesis of the disease. 4e28864e-982d-4fa9-a2c6-1e83fbaf0d86.paper_title: Kidney and endothelial injury biomarkers as predictors of complications and mortality in patients with malaria: a systematic review
4e28864e-982d-4fa9-a2c6-1e83fbaf0d86.text:
Malaria remains a major global health problem, with an estimated 263 million cases and 597,000 deaths worldwide in 2023 [ 1 , 2 ]. The burden is highest in endemic regions, particularly in Africa, while the Amazon region accounts for most malaria cases in Brazil [ 3 , 4 ]. Five species of Plasmodium are known to cause malaria in humans: Plasmodium falciparum, P. vivax, P. malariae, P. ovale, and P. knowlesi [ 4 ].

Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a frequent and severe complication of malaria, especially in Plasmodium falciparum infections, and is strongly associated with increased morbidity and mortality [ 5 , 6 ]. Clinical manifestations include oliguria, metabolic acidosis, and electrolyte disturbances, reflecting significant renal dysfunction [ 5 , 6 ].

The pathogenesis of malaria-associated AKI is complex and involves microvascular obstruction, hemolysis, systemic inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, and hemodynamic alterations [ 2 , 5 ] In addition to renal impairment, patients may develop anemia, jaundice, neurological dysfunction, and intravascular hemolysis, contributing to disease severity [ 1 , 5 ].

Methodological quality was assessed independently by two reviewers using:

For NOS, studies were classified as:

High quality (low risk of bias): 7–9 points.

Moderate quality: 5–6 points.

Low quality (high risk of bias): ≤ 4 points.

For MINORS, studies were classified as:

High quality: ≥ 17 points.

Moderate quality: 13–16 points.

Low quality: ≤ 12 points.

A qualitative synthesis was conducted following the Synthesis Without Meta-analysis (SWiM) guidelines. Studies were grouped according to predefined biomarker domains, including: Biomarkers of tubular injury. Endothelial injury biomarkers. Hemolysis and inflammatory biomarkers. Oxidative stress biomarkers. Additional biomarkers of renal dysfunction and endothelial activation. Inflammatory biomarkers. Associations with AKI, disease severity, and mortality were systematically summarized.

After removal of duplicates and screening of titles and abstracts, potentially eligible studies were assessed in full text. A total of 13 studies published between 2015 and 2025 were included in the qualitative synthesis. The study selection process is presented in the PRISMA flow diagram (Fig. 1 ).

dc0b12e4-c2f3-4ec1-9d82-888dfebe5738.text: The methodological quality of included studies was assessed using the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (NOS) and MINORS. Overall, studies demonstrated moderate to high quality. Common limitations included small sample sizes, heterogeneity in biomarker assessment, and limited adjustment for confounders. Detailed quality scores are presented in Supplementary Table 2 and 3.

120c7569-cb46-4c9b-8736-de93f36d43a4.paper_title: Kidney and endothelial injury biomarkers as predictors of complications and mortality in patients with malaria: a systematic review
120c7569-cb46-4c9b-8736-de93f36d43a4.heading_path: Results > Baseline characteristics of included studies
120c7569-cb46-4c9b-8736-de93f36d43a4.text:
The included studies comprised 10,332 patients, including both adult and pediatric populations. Most studies involved Plasmodium falciparum, although other species such as P. vivax and P. knowlesi were also represented.

Geographically, studies were conducted in Africa (n = 4), Asia (n = 4), Europe (n = 2), Brazil (n = 1), and multinational settings (n = 1). The incidence of AKI was high, particularly in severe malaria.

AKI definitions varied across studies. Most studies used KDIGO criteria, while others applied RIFLE or AKIN classifications, and a few used study-specific definitions based on serum creatinine thresholds or urine output. This variability may influence the reported performance of biomarkers.

eb8c1277-43f7-4620-abe3-a07c0017742a.paper_title: Kidney and endothelial injury biomarkers as predictors of complications and mortality in patients with malaria: a systematic review
eb8c1277-43f7-4620-abe3-a07c0017742a.text: NGAL levels were significantly elevated in patients with AKI and increased with disease severity, demonstrating strong associations with tubular injury and clinical outcomes [ 6 , 23 ] Elevated NGAL was also linked to hypoxic brain injury (PRR 5.5, 95% CI 2.3–13.2), suggesting a role in multi-organ dysfunction. Although NGAL is a sensitive early marker of tubular injury, it is not kidney-specific. NGAL is also released by activated neutrophils as part of the acute-phase response. Therefore, in the context of severe malaria, where systemic inflammation is prominent, elevated NGAL levels may reflect both renal injury and inflammatory activation, potentially limiting its specificity for AKI [ 6 , 23 ]

22462da6-4e33-4398-a930-9828daa17ade.text:
Biomarkers of endothelial activation and glycocalyx degradation were consistently associated with the development of acute kidney injury (AKI), angiopoietin-2 was identified as a robust marker of endothelial dysfunction and was significantly associated with the occurrence of AKI. In a meta-analysis including 7453 patients, elevated Ang-2 levels were associated with an increased risk of AKI (OR = 1.58; 95% CI 1.39–1.80), with consistently higher levels observed in patients with AKI compared to those without [ 24 ]. Syndecan-1, a marker of glycocalyx degradation, was also strongly associated with disease severity and renal dysfunction. Elevated syndecan-1 levels were independently associated with severe malaria (OR = 3.72; 95% CI 2.01–6.89) and correlated with markers of endothelial activation, including angiopoietin-2 and ICAM-1, as well as with serum creatinine levels. These findings support the role of glycocalyx breakdown as a central mechanism linking endothelial injury to organ dysfunction [ 21 ].

08d11fc9-45c4-4d28-81c5-0ed0dc644e03.paper_title: Kidney and endothelial injury biomarkers as predictors of complications and mortality in patients with malaria: a systematic review
08d11fc9-45c4-4d28-81c5-0ed0dc644e03.text:
Markers of oxidative stress, particularly F2-isoprostanes (F2-IsoPs) and isofurans (IsoFs), were strongly associated with acute kidney injury (AKI) and disease severity in malaria. Both biomarkers, which are products of lipid peroxidation, were significantly elevated in patients with AKI and showed robust correlations with renal dysfunction. In a prospective cohort study, levels of F2-IsoPs and IsoFs were strongly correlated with serum creatinine (r = 0.71 for both, p < 0.001), indicating a close relationship with kidney injury [ 18 ].

Importantly, these oxidative stress markers were also predictive of severe renal outcomes. Elevated F2-IsoPs and IsoFs were independently associated with the need for renal replacement therapy, with odds ratios of 7.37 (95% CI 1.86–29.23) and 5.50 (95% CI 1.76–17.24), respectively [ 18 ]. These findings suggest that oxidative damage plays a central role in the pathogenesis of malaria-associated AKI.

e6885528-94e3-4ecb-b9a9-44794d06c4a5.paper_title: Kidney and endothelial injury biomarkers as predictors of complications and mortality in patients with malaria: a systematic review
e6885528-94e3-4ecb-b9a9-44794d06c4a5.text: Pro-inflammatory and immunoregulatory cytokines, including interleukin-6 (IL-6), tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), and the IFN-γ/IL-10 ratio, were significantly associated with acute kidney injury (AKI), disease severity, and adverse outcomes in malaria. Elevated levels of IL-6 and TNF-α were observed in patients with severe disease and renal dysfunction, reflecting an amplified systemic inflammatory response. In addition, an increased IFN-γ/IL-10 ratio, indicative of a shift toward a pro-inflammatory state, was significantly associated with AKI and worse clinical outcomes, suggesting an imbalance between pro- and anti-inflammatory pathways [ 15 ]. TNF-related apoptosis-inducing ligand (TRAIL) is a member of the tumor necrosis factor superfamily that induces apoptosis through activation of death receptors. In the kidney, TRAIL has been implicated in tubular epithelial cell apoptosis and may contribute to renal injury in inflammatory conditions. Its role in malaria-associated AKI likely reflects the interaction between immune activation and renal cell death pathways. 6c06cbd6-fd6c-4b73-b557-1dcdc706705a.paper_title: Kidney and endothelial injury biomarkers as predictors of complications and mortality in patients with malaria: a systematic review
6c06cbd6-fd6c-4b73-b557-1dcdc706705a.text:
The findings of this review suggest that renal and endothelial biomarkers may improve early detection and risk stratification of malaria-associated AKI. However, their translation into clinical practice requires careful consideration of feasibility, particularly in resource-limited settings where malaria is most prevalent.

While biomarkers such as NGAL, KIM-1, and angiopoietin-2 have demonstrated moderate to good diagnostic performance in some studies (e.g., AUC values ranging from approximately 0.70 to 0.80), their routine use may be limited by the need for specialized assays, laboratory infrastructure, and trained personnel. In contrast, simpler and low-cost tools, such as salivary urea nitrogen (SUN) dipstick testing, may offer a more feasible alternative for early screening, particularly at the primary care level [ 12 , 24 ].

Therefore, the implementation of biomarkers should consider the balance between diagnostic accuracy and real-world applicability. In higher-level facilities, multi-biomarker panels may support clinical decision-making, including ICU admission and renal replacement therapy, whereas in peripheral settings, point-of-care approaches may provide greater impact.

1459fd50-1564-4a6f-8a1f-25d3d13fbf24.text:
This systematic review presents several strengths. First, it follows the PRISMA 2020 guidelines and was prospectively registered in PROSPERO, ensuring methodological transparency and reproducibility. Second, it integrates both renal and endothelial biomarkers within a unified pathophysiological framework, providing a comprehensive understanding of malaria-associated acute kidney injury (AKI).

Unlike previous reviews that focused predominantly on isolated renal biomarkers, this study incorporates markers of endothelial activation, glycocalyx degradation, oxidative stress, immune imbalance, and hemolysis. This integrative approach allows for a broader interpretation of the mechanisms linking malaria severity, microvascular dysfunction, and renal injury.

Additionally, the inclusion of both human and experimental studies contributes to translational relevance by bridging clinical findings with mechanistic evidence. The review also consolidates biomarker evidence across different Plasmodium species, increasing its external applicability in endemic and imported malaria settings.

0221b9eb-d270-4ce3-a925-55adb25e6126.paper_title: Kidney and endothelial injury biomarkers as predictors of complications and mortality in patients with malaria: a systematic review
0221b9eb-d270-4ce3-a925-55adb25e6126.text:
Although meta-analysis can strengthen quantitative inference, it was not feasible in this review due to marked heterogeneity across studies. Differences in biomarker assays, biological matrices, timing of measurement, and AKI definitions limit comparability, even when using standardized approaches such as standardized mean differences. Future studies with standardized methodologies and reporting are needed to enable robust meta-analytic synthesis.

Second, most studies were observational, limiting the ability to establish causal relationships between biomarker elevation and clinical outcomes. Third, several biomarkers lack standardized cutoff values, which may limit direct clinical applicability.

Fourth, differences in healthcare infrastructure between endemic and non-endemic regions may affect the generalizability of findings. Finally, publication bias cannot be completely excluded, as studies with negative biomarker results may be underreported.

Future large-scale prospective studies are needed to validate the prognostic performance of combined renal and endothelial biomarker panels and to define clinically actionable thresholds.

a6e14277-776d-48ed-99c1-addf42e8084b.paper_title: Kidney and endothelial injury biomarkers as predictors of complications and mortality in patients with malaria: a systematic review
a6e14277-776d-48ed-99c1-addf42e8084b.text:
Malaria-associated acute kidney injury (AKI) remains a frequent and severe complication, particularly in severe Plasmodium infections, and is associated with increased morbidity and mortality.

This systematic review suggests that renal and endothelial biomarkers may provide useful insights into the early detection and risk stratification of malaria-associated AKI. Tubular injury biomarkers, including NGAL, KIM-1, and cystatin C, were consistently associated with AKI, while endothelial biomarkers such as angiopoietin-2 and syndecan-1 were linked to disease severity and microvascular dysfunction.

In addition, biomarkers of hemolysis, inflammation, and oxidative stress were associated with adverse clinical outcomes, including renal replacement therapy and mortality. These findings support the potential role of combined biomarker approaches in improving clinical assessment.

However, the interpretation of these results should be cautious due to the observational nature of the included studies, heterogeneity in study design, and lack of standardized biomarker thresholds.

Further well-designed prospective studies are needed to validate these biomarkers, establish clinically relevant cut-off values, and determine their role in routine clinical practice.

fd3f96ff-0df7-4ade-83cf-3c0c9d49a770.paper_title: Diagnostic and Prognostic Biomarkers for Sepsis‐Associated Liver Injury: Current Status and Future Perspectives
fd3f96ff-0df7-4ade-83cf-3c0c9d49a770.text:
Sepsis remains a leading cause of mortality in intensive care units. In China, approximately 25% of ICU patients are affected by sepsis, which significantly worsens prognosis [ 1 ]. The liver plays a pivotal role in the pathophysiology of sepsis: It serves as a critical barrier against microbial invasion while simultaneously acting as a primary target of systemic inflammation due to its central role in clearing pathogens, toxins, and inflammatory mediators [ 2 ]. Liver dysfunction in sepsis is an independent predictor of poor outcome; once overt liver injury or failure occurs, mortality rates range from 54% to 68% [ 3 ].

The pathogenesis of sepsis‐associated liver injury (SALI) is complex and involves multiple overlapping mechanisms, including direct endotoxin‐induced hepatocyte damage, mitochondrial dysfunction, excessive reactive oxygen species production, lipid peroxidation, massive release of damage‐associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) (e.g., HMGB1), and activation of inflammatory cascades such as NF‐ κ B, impaired peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor‐ α (PPAR‐ α ) signaling, and NLRP3 inflammasome–mediated pyroptosis. A comprehensive understanding of these pathways is essential for identifying reliable diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers.

0345012b-476c-4444-a80e-2e0fe4f878df.paper_title: Diagnostic and Prognostic Biomarkers for Sepsis‐Associated Liver Injury: Current Status and Future Perspectives
0345012b-476c-4444-a80e-2e0fe4f878df.heading_path: 2. Limitations of Conventional Biomarkers > 2.1. ALT and AST
0345012b-476c-4444-a80e-2e0fe4f878df.text: ALT and AST are widely utilized biochemical tests for assessing liver function, having been in use since the 1950s and remaining standard practice today. Numerous studies have demonstrated that patients with SALI exhibit markedly higher ALT levels than those only suffering from sepsis. However, there are several limitations associated with ALT and AST testing. Firstly, these enzymes lack specificity [ 4 ]. While primarily associated with liver function, ALT is also present in skeletal muscle and cardiac tissue, leading to potential elevations during myocardial infarction or other muscular injuries [ 5 ]. Similarly, AST is predominantly found in the myocardium and serves as a crucial marker for myocardial infarction and myocarditis. Secondly, although an elevated ALT level is one of the key criteria for diagnosing SALI, it does not facilitate early identification of this condition [ 6 ]. Thirdly, both ALT and AST possess relatively long half‐lives. It is particularly notable that the half‐life of ALT can extend to 47 h, which makes them less effective in the real‐time monitoring of the progression of liver injury [ 7 ].

8a6c777e-aa1c-4809-99ed-0776ab547bac.paper_title: Diagnostic and Prognostic Biomarkers for Sepsis‐Associated Liver Injury: Current Status and Future Perspectives
8a6c777e-aa1c-4809-99ed-0776ab547bac.text: Bilirubin is one of the most frequently utilized biomarkers for assessing liver function and is employed in the SOFA. The Save Sepsis Campaign (SSC) guidelines suggest that serum bilirubin c o n c e n t r a t i o n s > 2 mg/dL (> 34.2 μ mol/L) be utilized as an indicator for identifying liver dysfunction. Another article defines SALI as a serum total bilirubin exceeding 4 mg/dL (> 70 μ mol/L). Although there is currently no agreed‐upon diagnostic criteria for SALI, most studies have tended to incorporate serum bilirubin levels in their criteria. Nevertheless, bilirubin still has the issue of a lack of specificity; for instance, hemolysis, drugs, and so forth, can result in the elevation of bilirubin. Furthermore, bilirubin cannot distinguish acute liver dysfunction caused by sepsis from preexisting chronic liver disease [ 8 ]. These are also reasons to attempt to discover more novel biomarkers.

fc8919b2-d531-47a8-9d07-f766364eebd0.text: MicroRNAs are single‐stranded noncoding RNAs that regulate gene expression by degrading mRNAs or inhibiting their translation. Owing to their encapsulation in extracellular vesicles or association with proteins, circulating miRNAs exhibit remarkable stability in blood, making them highly attractive as biomarkers [ 9 ]. e938f076-85d0-4cf7-9267-793f2cbaee95.paper_title: Diagnostic and Prognostic Biomarkers for Sepsis‐Associated Liver Injury: Current Status and Future Perspectives
e938f076-85d0-4cf7-9267-793f2cbaee95.text:
MicroRNAs are single‐stranded noncoding RNAs that regulate gene expression by degrading mRNAs or inhibiting their translation. Owing to their encapsulation in extracellular vesicles or association with proteins, circulating miRNAs exhibit remarkable stability in blood, making them highly attractive as biomarkers [ 9 ]. Hundreds of miRNAs have been implicated in sepsis‐related organ dysfunction, with miR‐122, miR‐155, miR‐30a, and miR‐103a‐3p showing particularly strong associations with SALI [ 10 ].

Overall, miR‐122 is currently one of the most liver‐specific and the earliest rising biomarkers in the SALI cycle, with performance far exceeding that of ALT/AST in multiple studies. However, its translation into clinical practice faces significant limitations. The detection process requires RNA extraction, reverse transcription, and qRT‐PCR or ddPCR, leading to long turnaround times, high per‐test costs, and a reliance on specialized molecular laboratories—resources rarely available on‐site in most ICUs. Furthermore, the lack of standardized reference materials or commercial kits confines its current use primarily to research settings. Until a fully automated, rapid, and cost‐effective detection platform is developed, miR‐122 will remain a powerful research tool rather than a routine clinical test.

f480d721-00fc-45da-990d-d39773079a83.paper_title: Diagnostic and Prognostic Biomarkers for Sepsis‐Associated Liver Injury: Current Status and Future Perspectives
f480d721-00fc-45da-990d-d39773079a83.heading_path: 3. Emerging Hepatocyte‐Specific Injury Biomarkers > 3.2. Hyaluronic Acid (HA)
f480d721-00fc-45da-990d-d39773079a83.text:
HA is a key component of the extracellular matrix and is particularly abundant in the liver [ 15 ]. It is synthesized primarily by hepatic stellate cells and cleared almost exclusively by sinusoidal endothelial cells. For over four decades, serum HA has been recognized as a sensitive marker of liver fibrogenesis and endothelial dysfunction. In chronic liver diseases such as viral hepatitis, alcoholic liver disease, and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, HA is one of the best‐validated noninvasive serum markers of fibrosis, offering higher sensitivity and specificity than many conventional parameters while avoiding the risks of liver biopsy [ 16 , 17 ].

In the setting of critical illness, HA also reflects acute sinusoidal endothelial and global synthetic dysfunction. In a large cohort of 1096 critically ill patients, Jensen and colleagues compared HA with bilirubin, albumin, and the international normalized ratio (INR). HA exhibited the greatest dynamic range and most accurately captured the full spectrum of liver impairment. Among HA, bilirubin, and the Model for End‐Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score, HA showed the strongest and most linear association with mortality risk [ 18 ]. These findings suggest that HA is valuable not only for the early detection of SALI but also for tracking disease progression and predicting outcome.

0e3c6fe4-ba3f-4f1e-ae4c-0a4c5e75db4a.heading_path: 3. Emerging Hepatocyte‐Specific Injury Biomarkers > 3.3. Glutamate Dehydrogenase (GLDH)
0e3c6fe4-ba3f-4f1e-ae4c-0a4c5e75db4a.text: GLDH is a mitochondrial enzyme involved in amino acid metabolism and is most abundantly expressed in hepatocytes [ 20 ]. Although present in other tissues such as the brain and kidney, its serum levels are overwhelmingly liver‐specific and are not influenced by skeletal muscle or cardiac injury, unlike ALT and AST. In a comprehensive evaluation of candidate markers for DILI, GLDH and miR‐122 outperformed all others. Notably, GLDH proved superior to miR‐122 in correctly identifying true DILI cases and demonstrated faster normalization during recovery from acetaminophen (APAP) overdose, even when ALT remained elevated [ 21 ]. A subsequent study employing random forest modeling confirmed that GLDH, together with keratin‐18 (K18) and miR‐122, provided the highest diagnostic value among tested biomarkers. A three‐marker model (GLDH + K18 + miR‐122) accurately distinguished hepatocellular injury from muscle, pancreatic, or renal damage and clearly separated healthy individuals from those with liver injury—advantages that ALT and AST alone could not achieve [ 19 ].

ee9627b6-8d39-4f37-b787-2d491be69f9b.heading_path: 4. Mechanism‐Reflecting and Prognostic Biomarkers > 4.1. Other MicroRNAs
ee9627b6-8d39-4f37-b787-2d491be69f9b.text:
Beyond miR‐122, several additional microRNAs have been linked to the pathogenesis and potential diagnosis of SALI.

miR‐155 is markedly upregulated during sepsis and contributes to oxidative stress and hepatocyte apoptosis. In LPS‐challenged mice, administration of a miR‐155 antagomir significantly improved survival and reduced ALT elevation by targeting Nrf2, thereby attenuating endoplasmic reticulum stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and apoptosis [ 9 ]. Although miR‐155 has shown excellent diagnostic performance in hepatitis C‐related hepatocellular carcinoma (sensitivity 72.4% and specificity 95.2%) [ 22 ], its role as a circulating biomarker specifically for SALI remains preliminary and requires further clinical validation.

miR‐30a levels are significantly reduced in septic patients compared with healthy individuals or those with SIRS alone, suggesting diagnostic potential [ 23 ]. Experimental studies in septic rats demonstrated that upregulation of miR‐30a, achieved through SOCS‐1 inhibition, suppressed hepatocyte proliferation, promoted apoptosis, and impaired cell cycle progression, confirming its active participation in SALI progression [ 24 ].

0ed169c3-f502-447d-88ff-ba30c2bfedb7.paper_title: Diagnostic and Prognostic Biomarkers for Sepsis‐Associated Liver Injury: Current Status and Future Perspectives
0ed169c3-f502-447d-88ff-ba30c2bfedb7.heading_path: 4. Mechanism‐Reflecting and Prognostic Biomarkers > 4.2. Differentially Expressed Genes (DEGs)
0ed169c3-f502-447d-88ff-ba30c2bfedb7.text: The identification of disease‐specific biomarkers through DEGs has become a widely adopted strategy in both oncology and critical illness. This approach has also been successfully extended to sepsis and various liver disorders. For instance, Li et al. revealed that MAPK14, identified through ferroptosis‐related DEGs, significantly influences the inflammatory response in pediatric sepsis and holds diagnostic value [ 27 ]. Similarly, Ke et al. confirmed that YOD1, GADD45A, BCL11B, and IL1R2 serve as robust prognostic biomarkers in adult sepsis cohorts [ 28 ]. In chronic liver disease, Govaere et al. identified AKR1B10 and GDF15 as progression markers in nonalcoholic fatty liver disease using DEG analysis [ 29 ].

04673774-9e0c-4c91-87d6-1477381990c0.text:
The identification of disease‐specific biomarkers through DEGs has become a widely adopted strategy in both oncology and critical illness. This approach has also been successfully extended to sepsis and various liver disorders. For instance, Li et al. revealed that MAPK14, identified through ferroptosis‐related DEGs, significantly influences the inflammatory response in pediatric sepsis and holds diagnostic value [ 27 ]. Similarly, Ke et al. confirmed that YOD1, GADD45A, BCL11B, and IL1R2 serve as robust prognostic biomarkers in adult sepsis cohorts [ 28 ]. In chronic liver disease, Govaere et al. identified AKR1B10 and GDF15 as progression markers in nonalcoholic fatty liver disease using DEG analysis [ 29 ].

Thus, among numerous DEGs evaluated in sepsis and liver injury, TNFRSF1A stands out for its liver‐restricted expression pattern and central involvement in key pathogenic processes of SALI. These findings position TNFRSF1A as one of the most promising DEG‐derived candidates for future diagnostic, prognostic, and even therapeutic applications in SALI.

3f37cef6-81b6-4254-aae2-9df14ccc48a3.paper_title: Diagnostic and Prognostic Biomarkers for Sepsis‐Associated Liver Injury: Current Status and Future Perspectives
3f37cef6-81b6-4254-aae2-9df14ccc48a3.text: HMGB1 is a highly conserved nuclear protein expressed in nearly all cell types [ 35 ]. Under physiological conditions, it stabilizes nucleosomes and facilitates transcription. However, during cellular stress or death, HMGB1 is actively secreted by immune cells or passively released from necrotic hepatocytes, acting as a prototypic DAMP that sustains inflammation via RAGE and TLR4 signaling [ 36 ]. Extensive evidence confirms its pivotal role in both acute and chronic liver diseases, where massive passive release from injured hepatocytes drives persistent inflammation and exacerbates tissue damage [ 37 ].

056446e3-8be9-40b8-8f9a-2f599e4865cd.paper_title: Diagnostic and Prognostic Biomarkers for Sepsis‐Associated Liver Injury: Current Status and Future Perspectives
056446e3-8be9-40b8-8f9a-2f599e4865cd.text:
HMGB1 is a highly conserved nuclear protein expressed in nearly all cell types [ 35 ]. Under physiological conditions, it stabilizes nucleosomes and facilitates transcription. However, during cellular stress or death, HMGB1 is actively secreted by immune cells or passively released from necrotic hepatocytes, acting as a prototypic DAMP that sustains inflammation via RAGE and TLR4 signaling [ 36 ]. Extensive evidence confirms its pivotal role in both acute and chronic liver diseases, where massive passive release from injured hepatocytes drives persistent inflammation and exacerbates tissue damage [ 37 ].

HMGB1 has been extensively investigated as a biomarker across diverse liver pathologies, including fibrosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, ischaemia–reperfusion injury, and DILI [ 42 ]. A meta‐analysis of 16 studies confirmed significantly higher serum HMGB1 in severe hepatitis B and acute‐on‐chronic liver failure, supporting its diagnostic utility [ 43 ]. In APAP‐induced liver injury, HMGB1 accurately reflects hepatocyte necrosis [ 44 ]. However, a major limitation is its relatively late rise; significant elevations typically occur only in severe or advanced injury, restricting its value for early detection of SALI [ 44 ]. Despite this drawback, HMGB1 remains a robust marker of inflammatory severity and a promising therapeutic target in SALI.

b0973323-412d-4d2a-84a3-fa4e24bec88a.paper_title: Diagnostic and Prognostic Biomarkers for Sepsis‐Associated Liver Injury: Current Status and Future Perspectives
b0973323-412d-4d2a-84a3-fa4e24bec88a.heading_path: 4. Mechanism‐Reflecting and Prognostic Biomarkers > 4.4. PPAR‐ α
b0973323-412d-4d2a-84a3-fa4e24bec88a.text: PPAR‐ α is a ligand‐activated transcription factor of the nuclear receptor superfamily that is highly expressed in tissues with active fatty acid catabolism, including the liver, heart, and kidney [ 45 ]. In hepatocytes, PPAR‐ α orchestrates all three major pathways of fatty acid oxidation (peroxisomal β ‐oxidation, mitochondrial β ‐oxidation, and microsomal ω ‐oxidation), thereby maintaining lipid and energy homeostasis. It also modulates lipoprotein metabolism, inflammatory responses, and insulin sensitivity [ 46 ]. PPAR‐ α is capable of alleviating acute liver injury. Some researchers have utilized fenofibrate (a PPAR‐ α agonist) to inhibit the acute‐phase response in the livers of mice [ 47 ]. Furthermore, studies have indicated that PPAR‐ α also plays a certain regulatory role in hepatic glucose metabolism. In mice treated with fenofibrate, the flux of glucokinase decreased, suggesting that the activation of PPAR‐ α has a negative influence on hepatic glucose uptake and glycolysis [ 48 ]. Consequently, the role of PPAR‐ α in diseases such as nonalcoholic steatohepatitis and cirrhosis has received extensive attention.

2edd3efa-229c-45a2-9dca-1b31124ef2a9.heading_path: 4. Mechanism‐Reflecting and Prognostic Biomarkers > 4.5. Macrophage Colony‐Stimulating Factor (CSF1)
2edd3efa-229c-45a2-9dca-1b31124ef2a9.text:
Macrophages constitute a cornerstone of innate immunity, playing essential roles in pathogen clearance, immune regulation, and tissue homeostasis [ 51 ]. In the liver, the macrophage pool comprises resident Kupffer cells (KCs) and monocyte‐derived macrophages (MDMs) recruited during injury [ 52 ]. These cells exert context‐dependent effects in both acute and chronic liver diseases: They initially eliminate pathogens and debris but can subsequently amplify inflammation or promote resolution and repair [ 53 – 55 ].

In SALI, resident KCs are rapidly activated and often undergo necroptosis or depletion, whereas circulating monocytes are massively recruited and differentiate into proinflammatory MDMs [ 56 ]. This dynamic shift is tightly regulated by CSF1 (also known as M‐CSF), which is markedly elevated in the circulation during liver injury due to impaired hepatic clearance and increased production by multiple cell types [ 57 ]. CSF1 acts via the macrophage colony‐stimulating factor receptor (CSF1R) to drive survival, proliferation, and differentiation of both resident and MDM populations [ 58 ].

be5bcc1a-0c43-49e9-8133-e03813b4c9b3.paper_title: Diagnostic and Prognostic Biomarkers for Sepsis‐Associated Liver Injury: Current Status and Future Perspectives
be5bcc1a-0c43-49e9-8133-e03813b4c9b3.text:
At present, no single biomarker can fully meet the needs of early diagnosis, severity assessment, and prognostic evaluation of SALI. Traditional markers such as ALT, AST, and bilirubin suffer from poor specificity and delayed elevation, while even the most promising new candidates (miR‐122, GLDH, K18, HA, HMGB1, and TNFRSF1A) have their own limitations, including differences in release timing, potential interference from extra‐hepatic sources, or inconsistent performance across patient populations.

Strong evidence now shows that combining several complementary biomarkers significantly improves both diagnostic and prognostic accuracy. The most robust and reproducible example is the panel of GLDH + miR‐122 + K18 (total K18 or caspase‐cleaved K18), which has repeatedly achieved AUC values above 0.93 in studies of drug‐induced and APAP‐induced liver injury and reliably distinguishes genuine hepatocellular injury from muscle, pancreatic, or renal damage. Although these data originate mainly from nonseptic cohorts, the underlying mechanisms of hepatocyte injury are highly similar to those in SALI, making the findings directly relevant.

cbc1ca10-0b5e-4699-ae9b-7d11e1dc7a9a.paper_title: Diagnostic and Prognostic Biomarkers for Sepsis‐Associated Liver Injury: Current Status and Future Perspectives
cbc1ca10-0b5e-4699-ae9b-7d11e1dc7a9a.text:
SALI remains a frequent and ominous complication in critically ill patients, yet it is still diagnosed late and imprecisely with conventional liver tests. This review highlights that several new biomarkers—miR‐122, GLDH, K18, HA, HMGB1, soluble TNFRSF1A, and CSF1—each address specific shortcomings of ALT, AST, and bilirubin, offering greater liver specificity, faster kinetics, or deeper insight into underlying inflammatory and cell death mechanisms. Although none of these markers is perfect in isolation, their complementary strengths provide a clear opportunity to move beyond single‐analyte testing. The available evidence strongly supports the superiority of rationally combined panels over any individual marker or traditional liver function test for the early recognition and risk stratification of SALI.

As summarized in Table 1 and illustrated in Figure 1 , each biomarker discussed in this review has distinct advantages and limitations in the context of SALI. These findings underscore the importance of a multimarker approach that combines complementary biomarkers to improve diagnostic accuracy and prognostic prediction. Large‐scale clinical validation of these multimarker approaches is now the critical next step. Successful implementation will equip intensivists with objective, timely, and actionable information, transforming our ability to detect, monitor, and manage SALI in routine critical care practice.

d2326874-21cd-4f50-b4b2-0d683ee74ac4.paper_title: The Efficacy of Gut Microbiome–Modulating Therapies on Liver Cirrhosis: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis
d2326874-21cd-4f50-b4b2-0d683ee74ac4.heading_path: MATERIALS AND METHODS > Data sources and search methodology
d2326874-21cd-4f50-b4b2-0d683ee74ac4.text:
The search for literature was performed using English databases, in particular PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and Cochrane Library, covering the period from January 1, 2000, to December 30, 2024. Two reviewers (Y.W. and J.O.) independently performed a literature search and evaluated the titles and abstracts of the identified studies based on the established inclusion criteria. When abstracts provided insufficient information, the full texts were reviewed to support decision-making. The third reviewer (Y.S.) assessed the disagreements between the 2 reviewers.

Probiotics were searched with probiotics; prebiotics were searched with prebiotics; synbiotics were searched with synbiotics; fecal microbiota transplantation was searched with fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT); LC was searched with liver cirrhosis and hepatic cirrhosis. Gut microbiome–modulating therapies and LC were used with the logical operator “AND”. Eligible literature underwent secondary screening through title and abstract review to identify clinical studies of interest. A full-text assessment was subsequently performed to select research meeting predefined inclusion criteria.

3dca321d-b20d-4b8b-92d0-353fea10a3b0.paper_title: The Efficacy of Gut Microbiome–Modulating Therapies on Liver Cirrhosis: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis
3dca321d-b20d-4b8b-92d0-353fea10a3b0.heading_path: MATERIALS AND METHODS > Study selection criteria
3dca321d-b20d-4b8b-92d0-353fea10a3b0.text: For analysis, clinical studies that satisfied the established inclusion criteria were chosen: (i) design of randomized controlled trials (RCTs); (ii) individuals involved in the study: The participants in the study included patients diagnosed with LC through histological or imaging techniques; (iii) intervention measures: placebo, probiotics, prebiotics, synbiotics, and FMT, without limitations on the specific components or duration of intervention; (iv) control group: All therapeutic measures, apart from the specific interventions, aligned with those applied in the experimental group; (v) 1 or more of the subsequent parameters have been assessed: alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), albumin (ALB), Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score, ammonia, endotoxin, inflammatory cytokines including tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α) and interleukin 6 (IL-6). All articles have been issued in peer-reviewed English-language journals.

e684de9d-3db9-4504-bfa6-720721eaa4e6.paper_title: The Efficacy of Gut Microbiome–Modulating Therapies on Liver Cirrhosis: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis
e684de9d-3db9-4504-bfa6-720721eaa4e6.text:
The eligible literature was determined based on the inclusion criteria, after which the researchers (Y.W. and J.O.) independently reviewed the complete text and extracted data with precision. Disagreements were addressed through discussion and consensus involving a third researcher (Y.S.). Data extracted encompassed study design, sample size, and specific details of the intervention (such as regimens and durations), along with the mean and SD of the intervention outcomes. In cases where the mean and SD were not provided, the estimated outcome was derived from the median, IQR, or range.

The risk of bias tool developed by the Cochrane Collaboration was used to assess bias in the included RCTs. Two researchers (Y.W. and J.O.) retrieved appropriate details and performed independent evaluations of bias risk. Discrepancies have been cleared up through clarification and validated by the additional researcher (W.L.).

5ef3def5-68b2-4a13-ae0c-4ac44a8530ab.paper_title: The Efficacy of Gut Microbiome–Modulating Therapies on Liver Cirrhosis: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis
5ef3def5-68b2-4a13-ae0c-4ac44a8530ab.heading_path: MATERIALS AND METHODS > Data synthesis and statistical analysis
5ef3def5-68b2-4a13-ae0c-4ac44a8530ab.text: Hepatic function indicators (ALT, AST, and ALB) were regarded as the primary indicators of outcome. Changes in MELD score, ammonia, endotoxin, TNF-α, and IL-6 levels were defined as secondary indicators of outcome. Continuous outcomes were presented as mean differences (MDs) in change scores with corresponding 95% credible intervals (CI). When outcomes were evaluated using various scales that lacked standardization, they were reported as standardized mean differences (SMDs). Clinical variation and heterogeneity between studies were assessed through inconsistency testing, local inconsistency testing, and loop inconsistency testing. A P -value of <0.05 was deemed a sign of statistically significant heterogeneity on behalf of the research investigations regarding the outcome. We made use of the surface under the cumulative ranking curve analysis (SUCRA) method in evaluating the efficacy of the treatments under investigation. The network forest plots were applied for illustrating the effect size corresponding to each study and treatment. Analyses were performed implementing Stata MP software (version 18.0; StataCorp LLC, College Station, TX).

6e8f777d-c43f-47dd-a8fa-6602d9da31de.paper_title: The Efficacy of Gut Microbiome–Modulating Therapies on Liver Cirrhosis: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis
6e8f777d-c43f-47dd-a8fa-6602d9da31de.heading_path: MATERIALS AND METHODS > Grouping of interventions
6e8f777d-c43f-47dd-a8fa-6602d9da31de.text: For the purpose of this network meta-analysis, interventions were categorized into 5 distinct nodes based on their therapeutic class and mechanism of action. Specifically, the nodes were defined as follows: (i) placebo: including placebo or standard of care alone; (ii) probiotics: comprising single or multistrain live microorganisms; (iii) prebiotics: involving nondigestible food ingredients; (iv) synbiotics: combining probiotics and prebiotics; and (v) FMT: encompassing the transfer of fecal matter regardless of the administration route.

f9667112-ce25-4a6e-891f-5da07bc5b646.paper_title: The Efficacy of Gut Microbiome–Modulating Therapies on Liver Cirrhosis: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis
f9667112-ce25-4a6e-891f-5da07bc5b646.text: After the full-text evaluation, a total of 17 RCTs on gut microbiome–modulating therapies for the treatment of LC were included ( 13 – 29 ). Figure 1 depicts the process of literature screening, following the review, evaluation, and discussion according to the inclusion and exclusion criteria. The electronic search manufactured 1,051 unique records. Screening and comprehensive analysis of full-text articles revealed 17 trials pertaining to 1,051 patients comparing 5 gut microbiome–modulating therapies or placebo. The evidence network for various outcome indicators is presented in Figure 2 . The sample size for the trial varied between 21 and 160 participants. A total of 12 studies evaluating the effects of probiotics, 4 studies on prebiotics, 1 study on synbiotics, and 1 study on FMT were included. No studies that met the inclusion criteria involving postbiotics as an intervention were included. The duration of interventions in the included studies varied, with most studies having an intervention period ranging from 4 to 24 weeks. Most of the studies used placebo or usual care as the control. Table 1 summarizes the fundamental characteristics of the included studies.

454df368-a53e-40be-9842-e34210052f72.paper_title: The Efficacy of Gut Microbiome–Modulating Therapies on Liver Cirrhosis: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis
454df368-a53e-40be-9842-e34210052f72.text: The evaluation of bias risk for all entailed RCTs is illustrated in Figures 3 a and 3 b. In conclusion, nearly all RCTs were assessed as having a low risk of bias concerning allocation concealment, blinding of participants and personnel, incomplete outcome data, and selective reporting. Two trials were deemed to have a high risk of bias for participant and personnel blinding. One trial was evaluated for unclear risk regarding allocation concealment and blinding, 1 for unclear risk in the generation of randomized sequences, and 1 for unclear risk-related to incompleteness.

e4c75742-fc76-4874-8c2d-b77949388fd1.paper_title: The Efficacy of Gut Microbiome–Modulating Therapies on Liver Cirrhosis: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis
e4c75742-fc76-4874-8c2d-b77949388fd1.text: The findings suggest that the overall heterogeneity of the study is minimal. The global inconsistency test indicated that group D exhibited a higher level of inconsistency ( P < 0.05) (see Supplementary File p1, Supplementary Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/CTG/B484 ). The observed differences between studies may be ascribed to multiple variables, including variations in interventions, sample characteristics, and measurement methods. Owing to the limitations of not being able to conduct loop and node inconsistency tests, it is recommended that future research or data collection be conducted to further validate the findings.

978268c4-c446-46ea-93b9-4a28ec101700.paper_title: The Efficacy of Gut Microbiome–Modulating Therapies on Liver Cirrhosis: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis
978268c4-c446-46ea-93b9-4a28ec101700.heading_path: RESULTS > Effect of gut microbiome–modulating therapies on liver function > Effect of gut microbiome–modulating therapies on ALT and AST.
978268c4-c446-46ea-93b9-4a28ec101700.text: A total of 4 studies examined the therapeutic impact of gut microbiome–modulating therapies on ALT and AST, with the primary interventions being probiotics and FMT. Analysis combining the network forest plots and SUCRA ranking results revealed that, for both ALT and AST, no significant statistical differences were noted in the MD and 95% CI when comparing the various intervention methods pairwise (see Supplementary File p1-2, Supplementary Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/CTG/B484 ).
