ba43c07b-51ba-4fbc-a36a-2ab8fe61a478.text: ROC curve analysis demonstrated that FF-LL showed strong discriminative performance for T2DM risk stratification, with an AUC of 0.816 ( Figure 4 ). The optimal cutoff value was established at 6.3%, corresponding to a sensitivity of 80.0% and a specificity of 87.0%. These results demonstrate that FF-LL can effectively distinguish T2DM from prediabetes in postmenopausal women with abnormal glucose metabolism.

8d9f1b3a-910c-4b65-82c4-d4a8581ccd44.paper_title: A dose-response study of the association between MRI-derived liver proton density fat fraction and prevalent T2DM in postmenopausal women with abnormal glucose metabolism
8d9f1b3a-910c-4b65-82c4-d4a8581ccd44.heading_path: Results > Mediation analysis of liver enzymes
8d9f1b3a-910c-4b65-82c4-d4a8581ccd44.text: Mediation analysis was conducted to examine the role of liver enzymes in the association between FF-LL and T2DM. The analysis was adjusted for age, BMI, TC, and L3-VFM, and a significant indirect effect was observed for ALT (coefficient = 0.01, P = 0.04), which accounted for 22.0% of the total association between FF-LL and T2DM ( Figure 5A ). Similarly, the AST/ALT ratio also showed a significant mediating effect (coefficient = 0.01, P = 0.04), which accounted for 24.9% of the total association between FF-LL and T2DM ( Figure 5B ). In contrast, AST did not demonstrate a significant indirect effect (P = 0.42; Figure 5C ). In summary, the pathway from hepatic steatosis to T2DM was partially mediated by markers of liver injury, specifically ALT and the AST/ALT ratio.

8b7ddb2c-65b5-4c9d-ad41-4e8809bf14ab.paper_title: A dose-response study of the association between MRI-derived liver proton density fat fraction and prevalent T2DM in postmenopausal women with abnormal glucose metabolism
8b7ddb2c-65b5-4c9d-ad41-4e8809bf14ab.heading_path: Results > Nonlinear association between insulin resistance and FF-LL
8b7ddb2c-65b5-4c9d-ad41-4e8809bf14ab.text: Restricted cubic spline analysis revealed a significant nonlinear association between the TyG index and FF-LL (overall P < 0.001, P for nonlinearity = 0.007) ( Figure 6 ). FF-LL did not change linearly with increasing TyG, but instead exhibited a distinct nonlinear pattern: in the TyG range of 8.0 to 8.75, FF-LL showed a mild initial decrease followed by a gradual recovery, with an overall small magnitude of change. Beyond this inflection point, the curve rose steeply, and the 95% confidence interval remained consistently above the 0 reference line, indicating a statistically significant positive association between high TyG levels and elevated left hepatic lobe fat fraction. The histogram in the figure illustrates the distribution of TyG index values in the study population.

45394dce-e062-4eaa-9f56-d2b940f80fa8.text: Our baseline analysis revealed that postmenopausal women with T2DM present a more adverse metabolic profile compared to women with prediabetes. Specifically, this profile is characterized by elevated lipid parameters, glycemic markers and increased insulin resistance. This finding corroborates previous studies ( 21 ). It can be attributed to the interplay between postmenopausal estrogen deficiency and the core pathophysiological mechanisms of T2DM. Estrogen loss exacerbates visceral adiposity, dyslipidemia, and insulin resistance. Meanwhile, the insulin resistance and beta-cell dysfunction inherent to T2DM further impair glycemic control and lipid metabolism. Together, these factors contribute to a more adverse metabolic profile, consistent with the established pathophysiological mechanisms underlying T2DM.

Our baseline analysis revealed that postmenopausal women with T2DM present a more adverse metabolic profile compared to women with prediabetes. Specifically, this profile is characterized by elevated lipid parameters, glycemic markers and increased insulin resistance. This finding corroborates previous studies ( 21 ). It can be attributed to the interplay between postmenopausal estrogen deficiency and the core pathophysiological mechanisms of T2DM. Estrogen loss exacerbates visceral adiposity, dyslipidemia, and insulin resistance. Meanwhile, the insulin resistance and beta-cell dysfunction inherent to T2DM further impair glycemic control and lipid metabolism. Together, these factors contribute to a more adverse metabolic profile, consistent with the established pathophysiological mechanisms underlying T2DM.

In conclusion, FF-LL is an independent T2DM risk factor, with a dose–response relationship partially mediated by liver enzymes (ALT, AST/ALT). At a cutoff of 6.3%, it shows good discriminative ability and a significant nonlinear association with insulin resistance. These findings suggest that FF-LL is a potential biomarker for T2DM risk stratification, though its clinical utility requires external validation in prospective cohorts.

7d962afa-f9f3-4b85-bf94-967b8102ef18.paper_title: Clinical impact of an EHR-integrated hyperkalemia management system: a real-world study of 10,934 episodes
7d962afa-f9f3-4b85-bf94-967b8102ef18.text: Hyperkalemia is a common electrolyte disorder associated with substantial clinical risks, including life‑threatening arrhythmias and even cardiac arrest in severe cases [ 1 , 2 ]. Accumulating evidence has linked hyperkalemia to prolonged hospitalization, increased all-cause mortality, and considerable economic burdens [ 3–6 ]. This electrolyte disturbance is particularly prevalent in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), heart failure (HF), and diabetes mellitus (DM) [ 7 ]. Moreover, the coexistence of hyperkalemia with these comorbidities further elevates mortality risk and exacerbates economic consequences [ 4 , 8 ]. Accordingly, early identification, diagnosis, and timely intervention for hyperkalemia remain critically important in clinical practice.

3498ffac-ab6d-4a6d-a687-80979fc41426.paper_title: Clinical impact of an EHR-integrated hyperkalemia management system: a real-world study of 10,934 episodes
3498ffac-ab6d-4a6d-a687-80979fc41426.text:
Hyperkalemia is a common electrolyte disorder associated with substantial clinical risks, including life‑threatening arrhythmias and even cardiac arrest in severe cases [ 1 , 2 ]. Accumulating evidence has linked hyperkalemia to prolonged hospitalization, increased all-cause mortality, and considerable economic burdens [ 3–6 ]. This electrolyte disturbance is particularly prevalent in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), heart failure (HF), and diabetes mellitus (DM) [ 7 ]. Moreover, the coexistence of hyperkalemia with these comorbidities further elevates mortality risk and exacerbates economic consequences [ 4 , 8 ]. Accordingly, early identification, diagnosis, and timely intervention for hyperkalemia remain critically important in clinical practice.

Despite its substantial clinical impact, research on standardized management protocols for hyperkalemia remains limited. This study introduces a novel management paradigm by comparing the diagnosis rate, treatment effectiveness, follow-up compliance, and disease burden before and after the implementation of the ‘Serum Potassium Management Center System’ at our institution. The aim is to establish an integrated approach encompassing diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up to minimize adverse events and reduce the clinical and economic burdens associated with hyperkalemia. Ultimately, this integrated strategy is expected to improve clinical outcomes and quality of life for patients with hyperkalemia.

3107dc47-9c79-479c-878a-0650e6ef6e8d.text:
Inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) age ≥ 18 years, and (2) at least one serum potassium level > 5.0 mmol/L during hospitalization. Patients were excluded if they had pseudohyperkalemia (e.g., specimen hemolysis, marked leukocytosis, or thrombocytosis) [ 11 ], malignant tumors, a life expectancy < 3 months, transfer to another facility during initial treatment, active infectious diseases, or a hospital stay > 90 days.

Clinical characteristics were collected separately for the hyperkalemia standardized group and the hyperkalemia routine group, including age, sex, height, weight, body mass index (BMI), use of renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system inhibitors (RAASi) or mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRA), disease duration, and laboratory parameters. Laboratory and clinical outcomes included admission serum creatinine, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), post-admission serum potassium levels, hyperkalemia documentation, administration of potassium-lowering therapy within 24 h, repeat serum potassium testing within 7 days, hospital stays, and hospitalization costs.

2d2eb11b-ec1b-4927-aeb1-0607d2d5dea0.text: Analyses were performed using SPSS 23.0. The Shapiro-Wilk test was used to evaluate the normality of quantitative data. Due to the non-normal distribution, continuous variables were expressed as the medians and interquartile ranges [M(QL, QU)] and compared utilizing the Mann–Whitney U-test. Categorical variables were presented as case numbers and frequencies (%) and analyzed using the Chi-square test. A two-tailed p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. To evaluate the independent association between implementation of the ‘Serum Potassium Management Center System’ and hospitalization outcomes (prolonged hospital stays and elevated hospitalization costs), binary logistic regression analyses were performed. Variables for inclusion in the multivariate models were selected a priori based on clinical relevance and existing literature. The models were adjusted for these predefined potential confounders. Results are reported as adjusted odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (95%CI), with statistical significance maintained at p < 0.05 (two-tailed).

63bc21d1-a411-4b27-8c3a-24a85f4aaa3b.text: The CKD subgroup comprised 86 patients in the hyperkalemia standardized group and 155 patients in the hyperkalemia routine group. Baseline characteristics, including sex, age, BMI, eGFR, disease duration, use of RAASi/MRA, serum potassium levels, and hyperkalemia severity grade, were compared between the two groups. No significant between-group differences were observed in any of these baseline variables ( p > 0.05) ( Table 3 ). After balancing for baseline characteristics, the hospital stays in the CKD subgroup were numerically shorter in the hyperkalemia standardized group than in the routine group, though the difference did not reach statistical significance ( p > 0.05). Similarly, hospitalization costs in the CKD subgroup were lower in the standardized group compared to the routine group, without achieving statistical significance ( p > 0.05) ( Table 7 ). In conclusion, the implementation of the ‘Serum Potassium Management Center System’ was not associated with significant improvements in hospital stays or hospitalization costs among patients in the CKD subgroup.

7dfa7d8e-bc6e-4fff-9c96-2b631fa14eda.text: The CKD-HF comorbid subgroup comprised 61 patients in the hyperkalemia standardized group and 111 patients in the hyperkalemia routine group. Baseline characteristics, including sex, age, BMI, eGFR, disease duration, use of RAASi/MRA, serum potassium levels, and hyperkalemia severity grade, were compared between the two groups. No significant between-group differences were observed in any of these baseline variables ( p > 0.05) ( Table 4 ). Following adjustment for baseline characteristics, the CKD-HF comorbid subgroup in the hyperkalemia standardized group exhibited significantly shorter hospital stays and lower hospitalization costs compared with the routine group ( p < 0.05) ( Table 7 ). In conclusion, implementation of the ‘Serum Potassium Management Center System’ was associated with significantly shorter hospital stays and lower hospitalization costs in the CKD-HF comorbid subgroup.

Binary logistic regression models were employed to identify factors associated with the hospitalization outcomes examined in this study, specifically hospital stays and hospitalization costs. The threshold values for prolonged hospital stays and elevated hospitalization costs were elevated based on the median values across all subgroups. Values greater than or equal to the respective median were classified as prolonged hospital stays or high hospitalization costs, whereas values below the median were categorized as short hospital stays or low hospitalization costs. Patients aged ≥ 60 years were assigned to the elderly group, while those aged < 60 years were assigned to the non-elderly group.

As shown in Table 8 , several factors were independently associated with prolonged hospital stays. A statistically significant overall effect was observed for comorbidities ( p < 0.05). Notably, patients with CKD-HF comorbidity and those with CKD-DM-HF comorbidity demonstrated significantly higher risks of extended hospital stays. Implementation of the ‘Serum Potassium Management Center System’ was associated with a substantial 27.3% reduction in the risk of prolonged hospital stays. Furthermore, each 1-unit increment in serum potassium concentration was independently associated with a 29.4% decreased likelihood of prolonged hospital stays. No significant associations were found between prolonged hospital stays and other examined variables, including age, BMI, eGFR, RAASi/MRA use, disease duration, or 30-day readmission rates (all p > 0.05).

As shown in Table 8 , several factors were independently associated with prolonged hospital stays. A statistically significant overall effect was observed for comorbidities ( p < 0.05). Notably, patients with CKD-HF comorbidity and those with CKD-DM-HF comorbidity demonstrated significantly higher risks of extended hospital stays. Implementation of the ‘Serum Potassium Management Center System’ was associated with a substantial 27.3% reduction in the risk of prolonged hospital stays. Furthermore, each 1-unit increment in serum potassium concentration was independently associated with a 29.4% decreased likelihood of prolonged hospital stays. No significant associations were found between prolonged hospital stays and other examined variables, including age, BMI, eGFR, RAASi/MRA use, disease duration, or 30-day readmission rates (all p > 0.05).

In this retrospective study, we investigated a novel management model for hyperkalemia by comparing the diagnosis rate, treatment rate, review rate, hospital stays, and hospitalization costs before and after implementation of the standardized management strategy.

Previous studies have demonstrated that rapidly rising serum potassium concentrations, prolonged hyperkalemia, and delayed follow-up monitoring are associated with an increased risk of adverse clinical outcomes in patients with hyperkalemia [ 13–16 ]. For example, among critically ill patients, a reduction in serum potassium of 1.0 mmol/L within 48 h has been shown to significantly decrease mortality risk [ 17 ]. However, hyperkalemia often has an insidious onset and nonspecific clinical manifestations, resulting in suboptimal rates of diagnosis, treatment, and follow‑up [ 13 , 18 , 19 ]. Even when hyperkalemia is identified, clinicians may not prioritize timely intervention, which may expose patients to an increased risk of adverse events.

45d7fb7b-87f8-41b7-9deb-484f472e5ee7.text:
In this retrospective study, we investigated a novel management model for hyperkalemia by comparing the diagnosis rate, treatment rate, review rate, hospital stays, and hospitalization costs before and after implementation of the standardized management strategy.

Previous studies have demonstrated that rapidly rising serum potassium concentrations, prolonged hyperkalemia, and delayed follow-up monitoring are associated with an increased risk of adverse clinical outcomes in patients with hyperkalemia [ 13–16 ]. For example, among critically ill patients, a reduction in serum potassium of 1.0 mmol/L within 48 h has been shown to significantly decrease mortality risk [ 17 ]. However, hyperkalemia often has an insidious onset and nonspecific clinical manifestations, resulting in suboptimal rates of diagnosis, treatment, and follow‑up [ 13 , 18 , 19 ]. Even when hyperkalemia is identified, clinicians may not prioritize timely intervention, which may expose patients to an increased risk of adverse events.

Collectively, these findings support a mediated causal pathway rather than a direct effect: the integrated serum potassium management system may indirectly reduce hospitalization costs primarily by shortening hospital stays, which subsequently curtails related expenses such as ward fees, routine monitoring, laboratory assays, and supportive care. In essence, the cost-saving benefit of the system is likely mediated through its impact on reducing prolonged hospitalization, rather than via a direct independent effect on medical costs.

0090af84-0dae-4d9e-9eff-034f69863c83.paper_title: Clinical impact of an EHR-integrated hyperkalemia management system: a real-world study of 10,934 episodes
0090af84-0dae-4d9e-9eff-034f69863c83.text:
This study has several limitations. First, this was a single‑center, retrospective study with a historical‑control design. Such a design is inherently susceptible to secular trends and unmeasured confounding factors, including temporal changes in clinical practice, staffing, hospital policies, laboratory workflows, discharge criteria, and medical financing systems, all of which may have influenced hospitalization costs and hospital stays. Therefore, definitive causal relationships between the intervention and the observed outcomes cannot be established.

Second, important baseline variables that may affect comparability were not fully available for adjustment, including admission service, principal diagnosis, acute versus chronic hyperkalemia, ICU admission, severity of CKD/HF/DM, acid‑base status, prior dialysis, medication burden beyond RAASi/MRA, and whether hyperkalemia was present on admission or hospital‑acquired. These factors may strongly influence management intensity and healthcare resource utilization, further limiting comparability between groups.

Third, subgroup analyses for hospital stays and hospitalization costs were exploratory and underpowered, and no adjustment for multiple comparisons was performed. Some statistically significant findings may therefore have occurred by chance alone, and these results should be interpreted as preliminary and exploratory rather than conclusive evidence of intervention effectiveness.

bfc2b368-449a-4af4-b904-06fe18703c8c.paper_title: Clinical impact of an EHR-integrated hyperkalemia management system: a real-world study of 10,934 episodes
bfc2b368-449a-4af4-b904-06fe18703c8c.text:
Hyperkalemia continues to represent a key clinical priority, with ongoing advances in its diagnosis, treatment, and assessment of its clinical and economic burden. Standardized management strategies are crucial for optimal care of affected patients. The implementation of the ‘Serum Potassium Management Center System’ represents an innovative approach to hyperkalemia management, offering a standardized model that was associated with improved diagnostic identification, treatment implementation, and follow-up testing rates in this study. The system was also associated with favorable trends in hospital length of stay and hospitalization costs in several high‑risk subgroups. Nonetheless, challenges remain, including inconsistent clinician awareness and non‑standardized approaches to hyperkalemia management. The standardized pathway enabled by this system may help overcome these gaps and streamline core components of hyperkalemia care.

Notably, this study was limited to process indicators and disease burden-related measures, and hard clinical outcomes such as mortality, arrhythmia, ICU transfer, or emergency dialysis were not evaluated. Therefore, the findings should be interpreted as observational associations rather than definitive improvements in hard clinical outcomes. Further prospective and comparative studies are warranted to validate whether this system can translate process improvements into better clinical outcomes, reduce the disease burden, and improve patients’ quality of life and survival.

3f5ffb88-0c71-4752-bb4e-d1e91699e94f.paper_title: Nonsteroidal Anti-inflammatory Drug (NSAID)-Induced Enteropathy Mimicking Crohn’s Disease: A Reversible Cause of Ileitis
3f5ffb88-0c71-4752-bb4e-d1e91699e94f.text:
Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDS) are among the most commonly used medications worldwide and are well recognized for their potential gastrointestinal (GI) toxicity. While upper GI complications such as peptic ulcer disease and gastritis are widely known, the distal small bowel is also an underrecognized site of NSAID-induced injury [ 1 ]. Current literature shows that distal GI complications are becoming increasingly more common; in fact, they comprise as high as 40% of all NSAID-induced adverse GI side-effects [ 2 ].

The presentation and findings of NSAID-induced enteropathy can closely resemble those of Crohn’s disease, particularly when ulcerations are localized to the terminal ileum. Both conditions may present with iron-deficiency anemia, elevated inflammatory markers, and small bowel ulceration, making differentiation challenging [ 3 ]. However, the clinical course and response to withdrawal of the offending agent can be critical in distinguishing between these two entities.

This case highlights the diagnostic dilemma of differentiating Crohn’s disease from NSAID-induced small bowel injury in an elderly patient presenting with chronic iron-deficiency anemia and terminal ileal ulcerations.

49e8b38f-5e89-456b-8609-99a9d2b164b7.paper_title: Nonsteroidal Anti-inflammatory Drug (NSAID)-Induced Enteropathy Mimicking Crohn’s Disease: A Reversible Cause of Ileitis
49e8b38f-5e89-456b-8609-99a9d2b164b7.text:
A 77-year-old male with a history of osteoarthritis, chronic iron-deficiency anemia (diagnosed four months prior to presentation) and prior small bowel obstruction status-post small bowel resection in 2022 presented for further evaluation of his anemia. Six weeks prior to presentation, he received an intravenous iron infusion after several years of oral iron supplementation.

The patient denied any GI symptoms like abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, early satiety, unintentional weight loss, melena, hematochezia, or diarrhea. He reported no recent changes in appetite or bowel habits apart from intermittent constipation related to his iron therapy.

bf7f5b00-db68-4d85-98fe-01d8e8fad695.paper_title: Nonsteroidal Anti-inflammatory Drug (NSAID)-Induced Enteropathy Mimicking Crohn’s Disease: A Reversible Cause of Ileitis
bf7f5b00-db68-4d85-98fe-01d8e8fad695.text:
A 77-year-old male with a history of osteoarthritis, chronic iron-deficiency anemia (diagnosed four months prior to presentation) and prior small bowel obstruction status-post small bowel resection in 2022 presented for further evaluation of his anemia. The patient denied any GI symptoms like abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, early satiety, unintentional weight loss, melena, hematochezia, or diarrhea. He reported no recent changes in appetite or bowel habits apart from intermittent constipation related to his iron therapy.

Review of prior endoscopic records revealed a colonoscopy performed four years ago that demonstrated aphthous ulcers in the terminal ileum. Given his history of chronic iron-deficiency anemia, previous small bowel resection, and colonoscopic evidence of terminal ileal ulceration, there was growing concern for underlying small bowel pathology as a potential source of chronic blood loss or inflammation, with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) being high on the differential.

316b8b4d-6db5-4d33-92e5-c0a4b20549bd.text: NSAID-induced enteropathy is an increasingly recognized cause of small bowel ulceration and anemia, often mimicking Crohn’s disease. The pathogenesis involves inhibition of cyclooxygenase (COX) enzymes, leading to reduced prostaglandin synthesis and disruption of the mucosal barrier [ 4 ]. 7b4fa148-291b-46ac-986d-e47315444e30.paper_title: Nonsteroidal Anti-inflammatory Drug (NSAID)-Induced Enteropathy Mimicking Crohn’s Disease: A Reversible Cause of Ileitis
7b4fa148-291b-46ac-986d-e47315444e30.text:
NSAID-induced enteropathy is an increasingly recognized cause of small bowel ulceration and anemia, often mimicking Crohn’s disease. The pathogenesis involves inhibition of cyclooxygenase (COX) enzymes, leading to reduced prostaglandin synthesis and disruption of the mucosal barrier [ 4 ]. NSAIDs also increase intestinal permeability by impairing mitochondrial function, allowing bile acids and bacterial toxins to penetrate the mucosa and initiate inflammation [ 5 ].

Complications of NSAID-related lower GI injury remain a significant clinical concern, as they are frequently overlooked or misinterpreted as inflammatory bowel disease. Failure to recognize this entity may lead to unnecessary immunosuppressive therapy, invasive procedures, or avoidable morbidity. Early identification and prompt withdrawal of the offending agent are therefore critical for optimal outcomes [ 9 ]. Current guidelines emphasize discontinuing NSAID use and reassessing inflammatory markers before diagnosing inflammatory bowel disease [ 10 ].

59c37b58-3b1c-4992-8c7b-17179822139f.paper_title: Nonsteroidal Anti-inflammatory Drug (NSAID)-Induced Enteropathy Mimicking Crohn’s Disease: A Reversible Cause of Ileitis
59c37b58-3b1c-4992-8c7b-17179822139f.text: In conclusion, this case shows normalization of the patient’s CRP and fecal calprotectin levels, along with resolution of ileal ulcers following meloxicam cessation. This case underscores the importance of considering NSAID-induced enteropathy in patients with terminal ileal ulcerations and chronic iron-deficiency anemia. The patient’s complete clinical, biochemical, and endoscopic recovery following discontinuation of meloxicam adds to the growing literature on how closely NSAID injury can mimic Crohn’s disease and demonstrates the value of medication review before initiating immunosuppressive therapy.

67989b45-e16d-49e8-bb14-bf17a145811a.paper_title: Successful reversal of hepatic visceral crisis in HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer: a case report
67989b45-e16d-49e8-bb14-bf17a145811a.text:
Breast cancer remains the most frequently diagnosed malignancy among women worldwide ( 1 ). Approximately 15–20% of cases overexpress or amplify the HER2 oncogene, a subtype associated with aggressive clinical behavior and a higher propensity for early visceral involvement ( 2 ). eaf10052-53db-4240-89bc-f199488e5f45.paper_title: Successful reversal of hepatic visceral crisis in HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer: a case report
eaf10052-53db-4240-89bc-f199488e5f45.text:
A 51-year-old Caucasian woman without relevant comorbidities and no history of tobacco or alcohol use, with a maternal family history notable for a grandmother with gynecologic malignancy at approximately 50 years of age and breast cancer at around 65 years, and confirmed BRCA wild-type status, was diagnosed in April 2016 with right-sided invasive ductal carcinoma, luminal B subtype, HER2-positive (cT1bN0M0). She received neoadjuvant chemotherapy with anthracyclines followed by weekly paclitaxel, after which she underwent breast-conserving surgery. Histopathologic evaluation demonstrated a pathological complete response (ypT0N0M0). Adjuvant treatment included radiotherapy, one year of trastuzumab, and tamoxifen.

In February 2020, a local recurrence was treated with radical mastectomy. Adjuvant systemic therapy was recommended but declined by the patient due to prior poor tolerance to chemotherapy; consequently, no anti-HER2–directed therapy was administered. By May 2023, a second locoregional recurrence appeared at the mastectomy scar. During the subsequent two years, the patient exclusively pursued non-validated alternative therapies (including ozone therapy and high-dose vitamin C).

47315a50-192b-41f8-8a8e-f46d7014ad8f.paper_title: Successful reversal of hepatic visceral crisis in HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer: a case report
47315a50-192b-41f8-8a8e-f46d7014ad8f.text:
Visceral crisis (VC) in metastatic breast cancer represents one of the most severe oncologic emergencies, defined by rapidly progressive organ dysfunction attributable to uncontrolled tumor burden. Among its subtypes, hepatic visceral crisis (HVC)—characterized in ABC-5/ESO–ESMO guidelines by a rapid rise in bilirubin >1.5 × ULN in the absence of obstruction or Gilbert’s syndrome—is associated with the worst outcomes ( 4 ). Real-world cohorts consistently report median overall survival between 4.7 weeks and 11 months despite aggressive treatment ( 5 ), reflecting its exceptionally poor prognosis.

The present case stands out because a complete and sustained reversal of HVC was achieved despite a biochemical profile far more severe than typically documented. Most published cases describe bilirubin values of 2–12 mg/dL at presentation ( 5 – 7 ), whereas our patient presented with bilirubin 31.4 mg/dL, AST 462 U/L, ALT 185 U/L, and LDH >1800 U/L—findings compatible with fulminant hepatic failure. Recovery from such profound dysfunction is rarely observed, underscoring the clinical relevance of this outcome.

b156b9ec-53da-4dfc-b61e-fdf40f99e12b.text: “At the time of admission, I experienced severe fatigue, abdominal discomfort, and progressive jaundice, which significantly affected my daily functioning. I understood that my condition was serious, although I was not fully aware of how critical it was at that moment. The initial phase of treatment was challenging, but I began to notice progressive improvement within the first weeks, particularly with the resolution of jaundice and recovery of energy levels. Over time, my condition improved substantially, allowing me to regain independence in daily activities. This recovery was unexpected given the severity of my initial presentation. I am grateful for the care I received and the treatment approach that was followed. I hope that sharing my experience may be helpful for patients facing similar situations.”

b20a00a1-7005-4cb6-9cfe-a14a6ac27245.paper_title: Autopsy‐Proven Immune‐Mediated Hepatitis With Rapid Liver Atrophy Despite Minimal Aminotransferase Elevation After Durvalumab Plus Tremelimumab Therapy for Hepatocellular Carcinoma: A Case Report
b20a00a1-7005-4cb6-9cfe-a14a6ac27245.text:
Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have become an established treatment option for advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), and durvalumab plus tremelimumab is one such regimen [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ]. However, immune‐related adverse events can involve multiple organs, including the gastrointestinal tract and liver, and may be fatal in some cases [ 6 , 7 , 8 ]. Immune‐mediated hepatitis is typically suspected when aminotransferase levels increase, and severity assessment often relies primarily on aspartate aminotransferase/alanine aminotransferase (AST/ALT) level elevation [ 9 , 10 , 11 ]. In advanced cirrhosis, however, aminotransferase levels may underestimate the extent of hepatocellular injury, potentially delaying recognition of clinically significant immune‐mediated hepatitis and leading to life‐threatening outcomes.

Herein, we report a case of a patient with steatotic liver disease–related cirrhosis who developed immune‐mediated colitis requiring high‐dose corticosteroids after ICI therapy while concurrently experiencing rapidly progressive liver atrophy and fatal liver failure despite minimal aminotransferase elevation. Serial non‐contrast computed tomographic (CT) imaging and volumetry objectively quantified progressive liver volume loss over time.

945190cb-193b-4e99-b6df-483a471f93e7.paper_title: Autopsy‐Proven Immune‐Mediated Hepatitis With Rapid Liver Atrophy Despite Minimal Aminotransferase Elevation After Durvalumab Plus Tremelimumab Therapy for Hepatocellular Carcinoma: A Case Report
945190cb-193b-4e99-b6df-483a471f93e7.text: A 71‐year‐old woman was referred for liver dysfunction in January 2018 and was diagnosed with cirrhosis attributed to nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (now termed metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis). On December 4, 2024, gadoxetic acid–enhanced magnetic resonance imaging showed that the largest HCC lesion measured 3.5 cm and that two additional lesions of approximately 2 cm were present, all confined to the right lobe, consistent with Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer stage B disease. The patient underwent transarterial chemoembolization on January 27, 2025. However, subsequent CT showed tumor progression, and the disease was considered transarterial chemoembolization–refractory. At baseline (Day −1), liver function was preserved with a Child–Pugh score of 6 (trace ascites) and an ALBI score of −3.27. The platelet count was 223,000/μL, and the FIB‐4 index was 2.01. CT demonstrated mild splenomegaly; however, no definite varices were identified on endoscopy or CT. Systemic therapy with durvalumab plus tremelimumab was initiated on June 10, 2025 (Day 0).

f9da9af3-e373-462c-b62a-9974cdf2cbdf.text:
This case is notable for the autopsy‐confirmed immune‐mediated hepatitis after durvalumab plus tremelimumab therapy, characterized by rapid progressive liver atrophy and fatal liver failure despite only modest aminotransferase elevation, whereas immune‐mediated colitis was controlled with high‐dose corticosteroids. In addition to serial non‐contrast CT imaging, CT volumetry provided objective quantification of progressive liver volume loss, strengthening the link between the clinical course and the pathological diagnosis.

We acknowledge that prior locoregional therapy (TACE) and the presence of multifocal HCC could have contributed, at least in part, to hepatic parenchymal loss. However, in this case, the tumor burden remained limited and confined to the right lobe, whereas serial CT and CT volumetry suggested progressive atrophy that was not restricted to the tumor‐bearing lobe. In addition, the autopsy demonstrated lobular hepatitis with patchy necrosis and CD8‐predominant T‐cell infiltration consistent with immune‐mediated hepatitis. Taken together, these findings support immune‐mediated injury as the primary driver of progressive liver atrophy and fatal liver failure, although a partial contribution from prior TACE or tumor‐related factors cannot be completely excluded.

7a6bcca1-f201-4105-ae13-8817d1dad122.paper_title: Prevalence, Clinical Profiles, Disease Severity, and Patient Outcomes of Alcoholic Liver Disease in a Tertiary Care Hospital of Nepal
7a6bcca1-f201-4105-ae13-8817d1dad122.text: Alcoholic liver disease (ALD) encompasses a spectrum of hepatic diseases caused by excessive alcohol consumption, ranging from steatosis to liver cirrhosis and hepatocellular failure. ALD is a significant global public health issue, particularly prevalent in developing countries, accounting for 11 million lost life‐years worldwide in 2019, which is even more than tuberculosis, cancer, and AIDS [ 1 , 2 ]. With alcohol consumption responsible for approximately 55% of total deaths and accounting for 9.5% of alcohol‐related disability‐adjusted life years, it poses a substantial burden on healthcare systems [ 1 , 3 ]. Early diagnosis and treatment that combines cognitive behavioral therapy and motivational enhancement with pharmacology are vital for improving patient outcomes [ 4 ]. This underscores the need for urgent and early intervention.

e8529d53-ec20-40bd-a12f-e940f072f179.paper_title: Prevalence, Clinical Profiles, Disease Severity, and Patient Outcomes of Alcoholic Liver Disease in a Tertiary Care Hospital of Nepal
e8529d53-ec20-40bd-a12f-e940f072f179.text: This study offers insight into the demographic distribution, amount of alcohol intake, clinical symptoms, biochemical parameters, and the disease progression in patients with ALD admitted to the tertiary care hospital of Nepal. The findings indicate that ALD is a prevalent health issue, with a rising global incidence of alcohol consumption over the last 20 years, particularly among the middle‐aged population. According to the World Health Organization (WHO) global burden of disease update, around 125 million people were affected worldwide by alcohol use disorders, 40.5 million people were moderately and severely disabled due to alcohol dependence and problem use, and 19.9 million years were lost due to disability due to alcohol use disorders [ 14 ]. The study has shown the male predominance for the disease; this difference in gender on alcohol consumption behavior can be linked to social and cultural norms, which identify males' drinking alcohol as normal behavior, while in the case of females, drinking alcohol is considered an immoral act and is prohibited in various households [ 16 ].

da687302-2d6c-4089-bc5a-493910175e65.text: This study provides clinically relevant insights into the prevalence, clinical profile, and outcomes of alcoholic liver disease in a single tertiary care center in Nepal, having higher prevalence of ALD as compared to similar studies. Multicentric large‐scale studies are required to validate these findings across diverse populations. The study underscores the prognostic importance of MELD scores, highlighting the early diagnosis and intervention. The results clinically underscore the value of referrals of patients for intensive monitoring and reducing the risk of mortality. The association between age, severity and the MELD score shows the importance of gender and age‐specific interventions and management. This study also highlights the importance of establishing routine alcohol use screening programs and the rising burden of ALD in middle‐income countries.

7c6724bc-a9ac-4f1b-90ed-3b045ae9621d.paper_title: Meropenem‐Induced Possible Mixed Drug‐Induced Liver Injury With Cholestatic Evolution: A Case Report Evaluated Using the Updated RUCAM (2016)
7c6724bc-a9ac-4f1b-90ed-3b045ae9621d.text:
Drug‐induced liver injury (DILI) is a leading cause of acute liver dysfunction and represents a major diagnostic challenge in clinical practice, as it lacks specific biomarkers and is largely a diagnosis of exclusion. Its clinical presentation is highly variable, ranging from asymptomatic elevation of liver tests to acute liver failure. Accurate identification of DILI requires careful temporal correlation with drug exposure, systematic exclusion of alternative etiologies, and structured causality assessment using validated tools [ 1 ].

Meropenem is a broad‐spectrum carbapenem antibiotic widely used for the treatment of severe and complicated infections, particularly in hospitalized and critically ill patients. It is generally considered to have a favorable hepatic safety profile, with transient and mild elevations in liver enzymes reported in a small proportion of patients. Clinically significant hepatotoxicity attributed to meropenem is rare, and only a limited number of case reports describing meropenem‐associated DILI have been published to date [ 2 ].

fb8b884e-0c3b-462d-b727-b3f699f3b4eb.text:

The updated Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method (RUCAM, 2016) remains the most widely validated and internationally accepted tool for this purpose, allowing standardized evaluation of temporal relationships, exclusion of competing causes, and response to drug withdrawal [ 4 ].

50b14bde-fd51-49ab-9705-fe95123563ac.paper_title: Meropenem‐Induced Possible Mixed Drug‐Induced Liver Injury With Cholestatic Evolution: A Case Report Evaluated Using the Updated RUCAM (2016)
50b14bde-fd51-49ab-9705-fe95123563ac.text:
A 33‐year‐old female presented to the emergency department with a 10‐day history of epigastric pain. The pain was dull in character, intermittent but persistent, rated as 8/10 in severity, non‐radiating, and associated with nausea, multiple episodes of vomiting, and documented fever reaching up to 40°C (oral). She denied changes in stool color, urine color, bowel habits, or weight.

Her past medical history was unremarkable. She had undergone cholecystectomy 12 years earlier for biliary pancreatitis. She denied alcohol consumption, smoking, use of herbal products, or intake of over‐the‐counter medications. There was no family history of chronic liver or hepatobiliary disease. Review of systems was negative for fatigue, pruritus, skin discoloration, arthralgia, or symptoms suggestive of autoimmune disease. There were no clinical signs of hepatic encephalopathy, including altered mental status or asterixis. Body mass index (BMI) and metabolic profile data were not available.

cb9dd362-3955-4bd8-8a58-05e7b0626458.paper_title: Meropenem‐Induced Possible Mixed Drug‐Induced Liver Injury With Cholestatic Evolution: A Case Report Evaluated Using the Updated RUCAM (2016)
cb9dd362-3955-4bd8-8a58-05e7b0626458.text:
Drug‐induced liver injury (DILI) remains a challenging diagnosis due to its heterogeneous clinical presentation and the absence of specific diagnostic biomarkers. Accurate diagnosis relies on careful temporal correlation with drug exposure, systematic exclusion of alternative etiologies, and structured causality assessment using validated tools.

The clinical picture of DILI varies according to the drug. Some studies use the term ‘signature’ to refer to the constellation of the clinical symptoms, pathological pattern, and a latency period. The most common signatures are acute hepatitis, acute cholestasis, or a mixed presentation. Other signatures include nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, fibrosis, microvesicular steatosis, and veno‐occlusive disease [ 5 ].

This case demonstrates a dynamic biochemical pattern, with mixed injury at presentation and peak, transient hepatocellular features, and subsequent cholestatic evolution during recovery. Formal causality assessment using the updated RUCAM (2016) yielded a possible association [ 4 ]. Importantly, this report uniquely incorporates liver biopsy, enabling distinction between background chronic liver disease and acute DILI. Prospective application of structured causality tools may strengthen future reports [ 6 ].

083c5f3c-0e2f-4e54-ba75-1842b9afe69d.paper_title: Co‐infection of Hepatitis A and E With Atypical Manifestation: A Case Report
083c5f3c-0e2f-4e54-ba75-1842b9afe69d.text: Developing nations such as Pakistan face a significant risk of infection from fecal‐oral pathogens like the hepatitis A virus (HAV) and hepatitis E virus (HEV), attributable to poor sanitary conditions and a lack of hygienic practices [ 1 ]. Hepatitis A is a well‐known cause of hepatitis around the world. It usually causes a short‐term, self‐limiting disease for about 4–7 weeks. The presentation is asymptomatic among young children, but acute liver failure and fulminant hepatitis in the elderly are among the symptoms, which also include fever, malaise, lack of appetite, diarrhea, nausea, stomach discomfort, dark urine, and jaundice [ 2 ]. Hepatitis E virus also develops a self‐limiting infection, but if it infects immunocompromised, or patients with pre‐existing liver disease. It can progress to chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, or acute liver failure [ 3 ]. HEV infection develops severe complications of liver failure and death if it infects pregnant women, especially in the third trimester [ 4 ].

90770f7e-d6e6-4ccf-9dcd-57f84969cdfe.paper_title: Co‐infection of Hepatitis A and E With Atypical Manifestation: A Case Report
90770f7e-d6e6-4ccf-9dcd-57f84969cdfe.text: A 14‐year‐old South Asian school‐going girl, previously in good health with no known medical conditions, presented to the emergency department accompanied by her mother with a primary complaint of progressively deepening jaundice over the past 2 days, preceded by a 5‐day history of nausea, repeated episodes of non‐bilious vomiting, and marked loss of appetite. She reported that the illness began insidiously, initially as mild queasiness and poor oral intake, which she attributed to eating street food after school. She continued attending school during the first 3 days of illness but noted worsening fatigue. On the fourth day, she noticed her eyes turning yellow and her urine becoming dark in color; this prompted her family to seek medical attention. She denied fever, pruritus, abdominal pain, distension, altered bowel habits, joint pain, bleeding manifestations, or changes in mental status. There was no history of similar symptoms in family members, no recent travel, and no use of herbal or over‐the‐counter medications. Her immunizations were up to date, and there was no known exposure to patients with jaundice.

7ad97af9-3c48-4e90-93b9-8321b107bd2e.paper_title: Co‐infection of Hepatitis A and E With Atypical Manifestation: A Case Report
7ad97af9-3c48-4e90-93b9-8321b107bd2e.text: “At the start, I thought it was just an upset stomach from something I ate, so I didn't tell my mother right away. When my eyes started turning yellow, I felt frightened, and I was worried it might be something serious. Staying in the hospital was scary at first, but the doctors explained everything to me and my family, which made me feel safe. I started feeling better after a few days, and it was a relief when they told me my blood tests and scans were back to normal. Now I'm more careful with what I eat and drink, and I always make sure my water is clean.”

9cca696d-dda2-48a6-bc66-428e6bc2b79c.paper_title: Co‐infection of Hepatitis A and E With Atypical Manifestation: A Case Report
9cca696d-dda2-48a6-bc66-428e6bc2b79c.text: This case underscores the need for clinicians to consider HAV and HEV co‐infection in patients who exhibit acute hepatitis, especially in endemic regions and developing countries like Pakistan. The subtle presentation of jaundice and the characteristic “starry sky” ultrasound pattern are important diagnostic clues. Improved sanitation, public health measures, and vaccination against HAV remain crucial strategies in preventing such infections.

dbcff441-f3b7-45ca-a567-8a47677c0e58.paper_title: Co‐infection of Hepatitis A and E With Atypical Manifestation: A Case Report
dbcff441-f3b7-45ca-a567-8a47677c0e58.text: This case report has several limitations. Firstly, as a single case study, it may not be generalizable to the broader population due to individual variability in clinical presentation and disease progression. Secondly, the absence of serial imaging or liver biopsy limits a more detailed assessment of the hepatic changes during recovery. Thirdly, diagnosis relied solely on serology (anti‐HAV IgM and anti‐HEV IgM); molecular confirmation via HAV and HEV RNA PCR was not performed. PCR testing would have strengthened diagnostic specificity, quantified viral load, and excluded potential IgM cross‐reactivity. This represents a meaningful methodological limitation that should be addressed in future investigations of atypical hepatitis presentations.

9119c6a4-4844-4979-b160-841495cf1ad7.paper_title: Co‐infection of Hepatitis A and E With Atypical Manifestation: A Case Report
9119c6a4-4844-4979-b160-841495cf1ad7.text: HAV and HEV co‐infection is associated with more severe clinical outcomes than either infection alone. A study from southern Mexico reported a co‐infection prevalence of 10% among children with acute hepatitis [ 7 ]. A hospital‐based study from Uttarakhand, India, found a prevalence of 5.9% for dual HAV/HEV infection among acute viral hepatitis cases [ 8 ]. A study from Bangladesh reported a co‐infection rate of 5.3% in a pediatric population [ 9 ]. Additionally, during and after monsoon seasons, seropositive results for both HAV and HBV were identified in 5.3% of dengue virus patients, highlighting overlapping water‐borne transmission dynamics in endemic settings [ 10 ].

8d35d52e-837b-445b-9b60-ca8ce978bc56.text:
HAV and HEV co‐infection is associated with more severe clinical outcomes than either infection alone. A study from southern Mexico reported a co‐infection prevalence of 10% among children with acute hepatitis [ 7 ]. A hospital‐based study from Uttarakhand, India, found a prevalence of 5.9% for dual HAV/HEV infection among acute viral hepatitis cases [ 8 ]. A study from Bangladesh reported a co‐infection rate of 5.3% in a pediatric population [ 9 ]. Additionally, during and after monsoon seasons, seropositive results for both HAV and HBV were identified in 5.3% of dengue virus patients, highlighting overlapping water‐borne transmission dynamics in endemic settings [ 10 ].

A unique aspect of this case was the liver ultrasound finding of a “starry sky” pattern. Hyperechoic portal triads caused by inflammation, periportal edema, and decreased liver parenchymal echogenicity that highlight the portal venule walls on ultrasonography are known as “starry sky appearances” [ 16 ]. A study from the Radiology Department of King Edward Medical University, Pakistan, found that 63.8% of the starry sky appearance was seen in the pediatric population with acute HAV or HEV infection, the third most frequent radiological finding among these patients [ 17 ].

3b74510e-7346-43f5-9cc7-69efb249c1a9.paper_title: Co‐infection of Hepatitis A and E With Atypical Manifestation: A Case Report
3b74510e-7346-43f5-9cc7-69efb249c1a9.text:
HAV and HEV co‐infection is associated with more severe clinical outcomes than either infection alone. A study from southern Mexico reported a co‐infection prevalence of 10% among children with acute hepatitis [ 7 ]. A hospital‐based study from Uttarakhand, India, found a prevalence of 5.9% for dual HAV/HEV infection among acute viral hepatitis cases [ 8 ]. A study from Bangladesh reported a co‐infection rate of 5.3% in a pediatric population [ 9 ]. Additionally, during and after monsoon seasons, seropositive results for both HAV and HBV were identified in 5.3% of dengue virus patients, highlighting overlapping water‐borne transmission dynamics in endemic settings [ 10 ].

A unique aspect of this case was the liver ultrasound finding of a “starry sky” pattern. Hyperechoic portal triads caused by inflammation, periportal edema, and decreased liver parenchymal echogenicity that highlight the portal venule walls on ultrasonography are known as “starry sky appearances” [ 16 ]. A study from the Radiology Department of King Edward Medical University, Pakistan, found that 63.8% of the starry sky appearance was seen in the pediatric population with acute HAV or HEV infection, the third most frequent radiological finding among these patients [ 17 ].

6f0272ce-c423-4dae-aa06-aeae8c7786ed.paper_title: Isolated Gamma‐Glutamyltransferase Elevation During Statin Therapy: A Diagnostic Pitfall and a Stepwise Management Framework to Prevent Unnecessary Discontinuation
6f0272ce-c423-4dae-aa06-aeae8c7786ed.text:
Statins, foundational pharmacotherapy for cardiovascular disease, exert their primary benefit by inhibiting HMG‐CoA reductase and reducing low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL‐C), thereby mitigating major adverse cardiovascular events [ 1 , 2 , 3 ]. Despite their proven efficacy, concerns regarding potential hepatotoxicity, often triggered by asymptomatic liver enzyme elevations, can lead to premature drug discontinuation. Isolated gamma‐glutamyltransferase (GGT) elevation poses a particular diagnostic challenge due to its multifactorial etiology, which extends beyond drug effects to encompass metabolic syndrome and systemic oxidative stress.

This ambiguity in clinical interpretation underscores the need for clearer management guidelines. Through a detailed case report integrated with a critical literature review, this article addresses three pivotal questions: First, what is the clinical significance of isolated GGT elevation during statin therapy? Second, what is its correlation with genuine hepatotoxicity? Third, could this biochemical anomaly reflect underlying cardiovascular risk? Our objective is to translate these insights into a practical, evidence‐based framework for clinicians, aiming to preserve the cardiovascular benefits of statin therapy while ensuring patient safety.

27500fcb-0d08-42b3-b06e-4155ed5b2c7e.paper_title: Isolated Gamma‐Glutamyltransferase Elevation During Statin Therapy: A Diagnostic Pitfall and a Stepwise Management Framework to Prevent Unnecessary Discontinuation
27500fcb-0d08-42b3-b06e-4155ed5b2c7e.text: A 69‐year‐old female presented in May 2022 with recurrent chest tightness and palpitations. She was diagnosed with coronary artery disease (CAD), arrhythmia (paroxysmal atrial fibrillation), grade 3 hypertension (very high risk), and primary hypercholesterolemia. The patient denies a history of alcohol use. Admission laboratory tests confirmed dyslipidemia: LDL‐C 3.61 mmol/L, total cholesterol 5.79 mmol/L, and triglycerides 1.4 mmol/L. Baseline liver function tests showed normal alanine aminotransferase (ALT, 29.0 U/L) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST, 25.0 U/L) levels, alongside a mildly elevated GGT of 79.0 U/L (reference range ≤ 50 U/L). Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a normal sonographic appearance of the liver, gallbladder, spleen, and pancreas. Atorvastatin (20 mg daily) was initiated for lipid management. Other medications included aspirin, levoamlodipine, and losartan, but no agents that can cause myopathy.

476e625f-622b-4b79-84a7-99c3de2dbff4.paper_title: Isolated Gamma‐Glutamyltransferase Elevation During Statin Therapy: A Diagnostic Pitfall and a Stepwise Management Framework to Prevent Unnecessary Discontinuation
476e625f-622b-4b79-84a7-99c3de2dbff4.heading_path: Discussion > The Clinical Significance of Isolated GGT Elevation During Statin Therapy
476e625f-622b-4b79-84a7-99c3de2dbff4.text: The epidemiological evidence further complicates a direct causal attribution. A large‐scale study found exceedingly low rates of significant, drug‐attributable transaminase elevation among statin users, though it did not assess GGT [ 13 ]. More instructively, research in a metabolically vulnerable NAFLD population that included GGT measurement found no adverse impact of statins on liver enzyme profiles [ 14 ]. These data suggest that in populations where background GGT elevation is common, statins do not appear to be a predominant driver. Isolated case reports of pan‐enzyme elevation exist [ 15 ], but they represent a distinct, acute pattern unlike the chronic, isolated GGT elevation seen here. We contend that the weight of evidence indicates isolated GGT elevation is a poor surrogate for genuine hepatotoxicity. Its diagnostic value is minimal without concomitant transaminitis, urging clinicians to look beyond the liver for its etiology—often towards underlying metabolic or cardiovascular risk.

d644b18d-2b19-46e3-a8d0-0e41024fb743.paper_title: Isolated Gamma‐Glutamyltransferase Elevation During Statin Therapy: A Diagnostic Pitfall and a Stepwise Management Framework to Prevent Unnecessary Discontinuation
d644b18d-2b19-46e3-a8d0-0e41024fb743.heading_path: Discussion > Assessing Correlation With Genuine Hepatotoxicity
d644b18d-2b19-46e3-a8d0-0e41024fb743.text: The first and most pressing question in this case was whether the observed GGT elevation represented statin‐induced hepatotoxicity. Formal assessment using established criteria for drug‐induced liver injury (DILI), such as the RUCAM scale [ 16 ], yielded a score of 2 (possible), argue against this diagnosis. The patient presented with two critical objective findings: first, a complete absence of elevation in ALT, AST, or bilirubin, which fails to meet the biochemical threshold for DILI; and second, and more decisively, the persistence of elevated GGT after drug withdrawal. This latter point is inconsistent with the expected course of a drug‐related injury, where improvement upon removal of the offending agent is typically anticipated. Therefore, both the cross‐sectional pattern (isolated elevation) and the longitudinal response (lack of normalization post‐cessation) provide strong clinical evidence that this was not a case of statin hepatotoxicity, corroborating the low risk profile indicated in current studies [ 17 , 18 ].

e0e43a43-5f0b-4416-bdc4-50eea61994a8.paper_title: Isolated Gamma‐Glutamyltransferase Elevation During Statin Therapy: A Diagnostic Pitfall and a Stepwise Management Framework to Prevent Unnecessary Discontinuation
e0e43a43-5f0b-4416-bdc4-50eea61994a8.heading_path: Discussion > GGT as a Biomarker of Underlying Cardiovascular Risk
e0e43a43-5f0b-4416-bdc4-50eea61994a8.text: For this patient, exhaustive clinical assessment during atorvastatin treatment excluded concurrent hepatic, renal, glycemic, or other hepatobiliary pathologies. The most instructive follow‐up finding emerged after drug withdrawal: both the elevated GGT and myalgia persisted unchanged for 7 months. When this temporal dissociation from statin exposure is weighed against the established literature, the argument for a direct drug‐induced hepatotoxicity becomes tenuous. Instead, a more parsimonious and evidence‐aligned explanation points to the patient's baseline cardiometabolic risk profile—encompassing underlying dyslipidemia and progressive coronary atherosclerosis—as the probable drivers of the persistent GGT elevation. Hence, the subsequent management strategy for this patient will focus on lipid‐lowering therapy, rigorous blood pressure control, glycemic monitoring, as well as weight reduction combined with dietary and exercise counseling.

b28b88d1-8e81-40ca-87d4-c01cd73ab832.paper_title: Isolated Gamma‐Glutamyltransferase Elevation During Statin Therapy: A Diagnostic Pitfall and a Stepwise Management Framework to Prevent Unnecessary Discontinuation
b28b88d1-8e81-40ca-87d4-c01cd73ab832.text: This case demonstrates that isolated GGT elevation in patients on statins can be a misleading indicator of hepatotoxicity and may instead serve as a red flag for underlying or persistent cardiometabolic risk. A knee‐jerk reaction to discontinue statins is therefore unwarranted and potentially harmful to cardiovascular outcomes. The stepwise framework derived from this case—involving verification of ‘isolated’ elevation, exclusion of alternative hepatobiliary causes, consideration of a monitored drug holiday for diagnostic clarity, a systematic evaluation of cardiovascular risk factors, and subsequent management strategy—provides clinicians with a rational approach to navigate this common dilemma. Future prospective studies are warranted to validate the utility of this management framework. Ultimately, this approach aims to shift clinical focus from a narrow concern over liver safety towards a broader optimization of global cardiovascular risk management.

3d9fa777-4a56-4150-ab85-00a1f8383eaa.text:
Breast cancer (BC) accounts for approximately 30% of all female malignancies and remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide [1] . In Jordan, BC is the third leading cause of cancer deaths, following lung and colorectal cancers [2] . Unlike Western populations, Jordanian women are frequently diagnosed at a younger age (typically between 40 and 50 years) and often present with more advanced stages of the disease [3] . This demographic disparity highlights an urgent need for optimized therapeutic monitoring and prognostic tools tailored to this specific population.

Despite advances in therapy, approximately 20–30% of BC patients develop metastases, with liver involvement drastically reducing the 5-year survival rate to under 10% [13] . Early identification of patients at risk of poor outcomes is therefore critical. To date, limited research has investigated the utility of liver-kidney composite biomarkers in the Jordanian BC population. This study aims to evaluate changes in hepatic and renal parameters before and after chemotherapy and to determine the prognostic significance of ACR, ALP/Cr, and ALBI scores for overall survival (OS).

fdf18aef-25a4-4b60-a86c-5edf1eb28ed9.paper_title: Assessing the hepatic and renal parameters of breast cancer patient blood samples before and after chemotherapy
fdf18aef-25a4-4b60-a86c-5edf1eb28ed9.text: This retrospective cohort study was performed at King Abdullah University Hospital (KAUH), a prominent tertiary care and educational institution in Irbid, Jordan. The study period spanned from January 2011 to April 2025. The study protocol received approval from the KAUH Institutional Review Board (IRB) (Reference No. 8/175/2024). Due to the study's retrospective design and the use of anonymized data from existing medical records, the IRB deemed specific patient consent unnecessary.

43207adb-123c-48b5-9198-133d46d61298.paper_title: Assessing the hepatic and renal parameters of breast cancer patient blood samples before and after chemotherapy
43207adb-123c-48b5-9198-133d46d61298.text:
The medical records of approximately 2500 patients diagnosed with BC and treated at KAUH from January 2011 to April 2025 were initially assessed for eligibility. An exhaustive and methodical data collection strategy was employed to ensure the quality and comprehensiveness of the data for the analysis, thereby bolstering confidence in the study's methodology and conclusions.

Patients qualified for the study if they possessed a histologically verified diagnosis of BC, had received systemic chemotherapy in the neoadjuvant, adjuvant, or palliative settings, and had complete LFT and KFT results accessible both before chemotherapy and following four cycles of chemotherapy. Furthermore, qualifying patients needed sufficient follow-up data to determine their OS status.

Patients were excluded from the final analysis if they met multiple predetermined criteria. This encompassed incomplete or unreliable clinicopathological data, including missing final tumor staging information; unavailable estrogen receptor (ER) or progesterone receptor (PR) test results; or ambiguous Human Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor 2 (HER2) status without confirming fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) testing or with absent FISH results. Patients were excluded if treatment details were either undocumented or incomplete; for instance, if the chemotherapy regimen was not recorded, if the patient had a history of radiation therapy, or if critical information regarding surgical interventions was absent when necessary for staging or outcome evaluation.

de91e0d7-97d0-4386-ace8-093a82b18d8f.heading_path: Methods > Data collection and laboratory measurements
de91e0d7-97d0-4386-ace8-093a82b18d8f.text:
Clinical and demographic data were extracted from electronic medical records, including age, smoking status, tumor histology (type and grade), tumor laterality, and receptor status (ER, PR, and HER2).

Biochemical parameters were recorded at baseline (pre-chemotherapy) and post-treatment. Hepatic parameters included total protein, albumin, total bilirubin, direct bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase (ALP), alanine transaminase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), and gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT). Renal parameters included serum urea, creatinine (Cr), sodium (Na + ), and potassium (K + ).

8c868d7c-8768-4f69-a459-7958885551d8.paper_title: Assessing the hepatic and renal parameters of breast cancer patient blood samples before and after chemotherapy
8c868d7c-8768-4f69-a459-7958885551d8.text: All statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics version 27. The distribution of variables was examined using the Shapiro–Wilk and Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests. Non-normally distributed continuous variables were summarized as medians with interquartile ranges (IQR), while categorical variables were presented as frequencies and percentages. Baseline differences between the low- and high-ACR groups were assessed using the Mann–Whitney U test for continuous variables and the Chi-square or Fisher’s exact test for categorical variables. Changes in liver and kidney function parameters before and after chemotherapy—including total protein, albumin, bilirubin (total and direct), ALP, ALT, AST, Cr, urea, Na+ , and K+ ; as well as composite indices (ACR, ALBI, and the ALP/creatinine (ALP/Cr) ratios) were evaluated using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, with Z statistics and p -values reported.

ca1fb317-dd9d-4df0-89a6-fdb4514bf292.paper_title: Assessing the hepatic and renal parameters of breast cancer patient blood samples before and after chemotherapy
ca1fb317-dd9d-4df0-89a6-fdb4514bf292.text: In this study, the longitudinal variation in liver and kidney function parameters after chemotherapy in BC patients was assessed, and the prognostic value of composite liver–kidney biomarkers was investigated. Our findings demonstrate that, despite the stable levels of conventional LFTs and KFTs post-chemotherapy, composite indices integrating liver and renal parameters—particularly the ACR and the ALP/Cr — were significantly different and strongly associated with OS. These findings suggest the potential of composite biomarkers for detecting subtle physiological stress across multiple organs that individual biomarkers might miss. Additionally, the findings reinforce the concept that cancer prognosis is driven not only by tumor characteristics but also by systemic host responses involving nutrition, inflammation, muscle mass, hepatic metabolism, and renal function.

15a673bf-90aa-4b9f-a925-af17b8e15663.paper_title: Assessing the hepatic and renal parameters of breast cancer patient blood samples before and after chemotherapy
15a673bf-90aa-4b9f-a925-af17b8e15663.text:
In this study, the longitudinal variation in liver and kidney function parameters after chemotherapy in BC patients was assessed, and the prognostic value of composite liver–kidney biomarkers was investigated. Our findings demonstrate that, despite the stable levels of conventional LFTs and KFTs post-chemotherapy, composite indices integrating liver and renal parameters—particularly the ACR and the ALP/Cr — were significantly different and strongly associated with OS. These findings suggest the potential of composite biomarkers for detecting subtle physiological stress across multiple organs that individual biomarkers might miss. Additionally, the findings reinforce the concept that cancer prognosis is driven not only by tumor characteristics but also by systemic host responses involving nutrition, inflammation, muscle mass, hepatic metabolism, and renal function.

Similarly, the small but statistically significant decrease in serum creatinine post-chemotherapy likely reflects changes in muscle mass rather than improved renal function. Serum creatinine is influenced by skeletal muscle turnover, and anticancer-associated or chemotherapy-induced generalized muscle loss and wasting as a source of the artificial lowering of the serum concentration of creatinine in cancer patients, despite the presence and retention of preserved renal reserve [22] , [23] . This phenomenon has been well described in oncology populations and underscores the limitation of creatinine as a standalone marker of kidney function in cancer patients [24] .

c776e88d-e511-4bf7-b0e1-7015bee5fce8.paper_title: Assessing the hepatic and renal parameters of breast cancer patient blood samples before and after chemotherapy
c776e88d-e511-4bf7-b0e1-7015bee5fce8.text:
In conclusion, this study clearly illustrates that composite liver and kidney indices, particularly ACR and ALP/Cr, which are important for the prognosis of BC patients receiving chemotherapy, provide more than conventional liver or kidney function indices alone. While routine LFTs and KFTs remained largely stable post treatment—indicating preserved organ integrity—significant alterations in composite indices revealed subclinical systemic stress that translated into marked differences in OS.

The high survival ratio between post- and pre-treatment ACR and ALP/Cr levels clearly illustrates the need to combine variables that reflect hepatic synthetic function, renal excretion, muscle mass, and metabolism for the evaluation and risk assessment of malignancies. Moreover, the ALBI did not show a significant impact on discriminating survival differences and may reflect that current liver-specific scoring systems lack sensitivity in noncirrhotic breast cancer patients. Taken together, these data clearly demonstrate the potential utility and efficacy of composite multi-organ indices as cost-effective, feasible prognostic variables for discriminating between poor and favorable outcomes following chemotherapy.

c9580373-9ae7-4338-a79a-e321381564a9.paper_title: A Microsimulation-Based Approach for Mitigating Societal Bias in Chronic Kidney Disease Data
c9580373-9ae7-4338-a79a-e321381564a9.text: Our primary data source is the American Family Cohort (AFC), which is a research version of a Center for Medicare and Medicaid Services–certified clinical registry and the largest primary care registry in the United States. 46 The AFC includes clinical, social, and demographic information for more than 7 million individuals and 1,300 practices, representing all 50 states. The dataset has a high representation of underserved (e.g., racial and ethnic minority, rural, and low-income) populations and includes individuals insured through Medicare and Medicaid as well as privately. We used these primary care registry data to characterize stages of CKD progression, including among undiagnosed patients.

ddff8a46-c8ca-4961-91f8-314fa5ecf9a0.paper_title: A Microsimulation-Based Approach for Mitigating Societal Bias in Chronic Kidney Disease Data

b03b29b5-be35-4dcb-aa60-d1e0598da982.paper_title: A Microsimulation-Based Approach for Mitigating Societal Bias in Chronic Kidney Disease Data
b03b29b5-be35-4dcb-aa60-d1e0598da982.heading_path: Methods > Data > Social drivers of health
b03b29b5-be35-4dcb-aa60-d1e0598da982.text: In addition to the AFC dataset, we considered 2 census tract–level indices of social deprivation and vulnerability: the Index of Concentration at the Extremes (ICE) and the Social Deprivation Index (SDI). 49 , 50 These indices were generated using the 2020 American Community Survey data 51 and assigned to individual patients based on census tracts. Individuals missing census tract information were excluded from the calculation of ICE and SDI calibration targets. The indices were selected to capture relationships between social factors known to affect the progression of CKD, based on prior literature. 11 , 26 – 28 , 52 The ICE is a metric expressing concentrated extremes of both privilege and deprivation. Three types of ICE are available: income inequality, racial composition, or combined income and race. We used the latter, which jointly measures economic and racial segregation. For a given geographic area and population, it compares the fraction of non-Hispanic Whites who are above the 80th percentile of income nationally with the fraction of non-White minorities whose income is below the 20th percentile. The SDI was developed to identify areas with unmet health care access needs for additional resource allocation. It is based on data regarding education, employment, family composition, housing quality, income, and transportation. We mapped the values of both indices into 3 quantiles based on their distribution in the AFC dataset.

a158c6d5-7edd-411c-9dec-b675d38b87bb.text: There are 2 primary simulation modeling approaches for CKD. 53 , 54 The first creates discrete-time transitions through CKD disease states, defined by transition probabilities or risk equations. 55 , 56 The second considers continuous, linear eGFR decline, with decline rates typically sampled from predefined distributions. 57 , 58 Both approaches allow for modeling changes in progression associated with time-dependent changes to diagnosed comorbidities, CKD diagnosis status, and interventions, such as particular treatments. However, because CKD disease states are defined by eGFR values in clinical practice, directly modeling eGFR decline is, in principle, clinically better motivated than discrete stage modeling.

Rates of eGFR decline conditional on diabetes, hypertension, and CKD stage could not be directly estimated from the data. To obtain them, we instead used a Bayesian calibration procedure using calibration targets derived from the AFC dataset, as illustrated in Figure 3 . The targets reflect age-specific distributions of CKD stages by sex, diabetes, hypertension status, ICE quantiles, and SDI quantiles (Parameters Supplement).

For all calibrated parameters, we defined truncated univariate normal prior distributions to exclude eGFR slopes indicating improvement over time, based on existing evidence, theory, and plausibility ( Supplementary Table S3 ). We applied a standard deviation corresponding to the coefficient of variation of 0.308 for sampling parameters. This coefficient corresponds to a standard deviation of 0.20 in the rate of progression among healthy individuals and captures the range of yearly rates of progression among healthy individuals reported in past literature. 57 For combinations of covariates not previously reported (e.g., co-occurrence of diabetes and hypertension), we used the higher mean prior values corresponding to either one of the conditions occurring and applied a higher coefficient of variation (0.461) to indicate a lower level of confidence in the priors. We further adjusted truncated normal priors based on regression analysis to achieve coverage of calibration targets.

2a6f0344-ed3b-47e5-9622-3b8a08c4af38.paper_title: A Microsimulation-Based Approach for Mitigating Societal Bias in Chronic Kidney Disease Data
2a6f0344-ed3b-47e5-9622-3b8a08c4af38.text: We extracted a cohort of 733,337 individuals from the AFC dataset, described in Table 1 . A cohort extraction flowchart also appears in the Figures and Tables Supplement. The cohort had a mean age of 60 y and was 44% male. At inclusion, 8% of individuals had a CKD diagnosis code. This is lower than the national age-adjusted prevalence of 21% but consistent with a high degree of underdiagnosis of CKD. 12 , 67 , 68 In addition, 25% of individuals had a diabetes diagnosis and 60% had a hypertension diagnosis, similar to national prevalence values. Our cohort had 88% of individuals with an eGFR value at or above 60, corresponding to no CKD or stages 1 and 2. 61 , 62 Only 6% of our cohort was Black or African American, with 79% White individuals. Of note, 12% of the cohort were missing race, 27% were missing ethnicity information, and 15% had missing census tract information. For the social indices, ICE and SDI, we observed a health gradient, in which indices indicating higher levels of deprivation were associated with a higher prevalence of diabetes, hypertension, and CKD. For instance, the prevalence of diabetes ranged from 19% to 31% in the least and most deprived ICE quantile, respectively.

3e58bf52-f984-4241-b42e-52c5d8c2dcf5.text: Our calibration procedure generated a single best-fitting parameter set, which we refer to as the mean posterior. The inclusion of ICE and SDI calibration targets did not affect the value of the mean posterior. Figure 4 shows the value of the mean posterior compared with the mean prior slope parameters as well as the distribution of sampled parameters. The mean baseline rate of decline among healthy individuals was 0.68 mL/min/1.73 m 2 , 5% higher than that in the prior, and increased by 13% after reaching CKD stage 3a (compared with no change in the prior). Decline prior to CKD stage 3a was elevated 1% by comorbid diabetes, 15% by hypertension, and 159% by a combination of both (compared with 69%, 11%, and 69% increase in the prior). 6677f130-957e-4195-b818-229d1e25edf7.paper_title: A Microsimulation-Based Approach for Mitigating Societal Bias in Chronic Kidney Disease Data
6677f130-957e-4195-b818-229d1e25edf7.text:
We studied the effect of the 2021 removal of race adjustment from the eGFR equation in order to understand its impact on clinical outcomes and generate debiased data simulations that reflect the effect of equation change on disease trajectories change. This involved creating a microsimulation model of CKD progression based on eGFR decline over time, calibrated to a cohort of patients in a large primary care dataset. Our model was able to reproduce stage distributions observed in the cohort, which reflected patterns of CKD progression and care informed by the 2009 CKD-EPI equation.

The model allows for generating counterfactual eGFR trajectories that reflect the use of the 2021 CKD-EPI equation through adjusting the timing of interventions based on the counterfactual eGFR levels. The trajectories simulated under the counterfactual scenario reflected earlier diagnoses for Black patients and later diagnoses for non-Black patients than those observed in the data. However, these changes led to differences in life expectancy not exceeding 2 mo among those with CKD. While these results were sensitive to assumptions on the rate of diagnosis and intervention effectiveness, the simulated effect among those with CKD did not exceed 4.2 mo even under assumptions of universal diagnosis and treatment initiated at stage 3a.

9157eda5-7caf-403f-87ce-9a5715f5631f.text: Although in this case the SWM did not transform into lymphoma but rather progressed from MDS to AML, insights can be drawn from literature on WM transforming into DLBCL. A 2026 study in Leukemia further demonstrated that BTKi-based immunochemotherapy regimens (such as ZR-CHOP) can significantly improve survival in WM patients, with particularly pronounced benefits for those with non-GCB subtype, double-expression, or extranodal involvement ( 18 ). Moreover, transformation events can occur at any stage of the disease, even during BTKi treatment. From a molecular perspective, the MYD88 L265P mutation may serve as the molecular basis for WM transformation, while mutations in CXCR4, TP53, and others drive clonal evolution ( 19 ). In this case, the B-lymphoid lineage harbored MYD88 and CXCR4 mutations, suggesting that similar molecular mechanisms may contribute to clonal evolution. Even though the disease ultimately progressed to myeloid leukemia rather than lymphoma, this highlights the genetic instability of smoldering WM during the latent phase and the inherent risk of disease progression.

8b64bcb7-240e-419c-ab44-c6e27795b8ce.text: Very severe aplastic anemia (VSAA) is a life-threatening bone marrow failure disorder. Allogeneic HSCT is curative but often unavailable ( 1 ).
